{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"🖥️ Frontend Architecture Scoping","url":"https://app.notion.com/p/3bb830e8fbaa8188adf2c6bfebf67ed5?pvs=204","text":"Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3bb830e8fbaa8188adf2c6bfebf67ed5 as of 2026-08-13T20:06:40.763Z: {"title":"Frontend Architecture Scoping"} {"type":"emoji","emoji":"🖥️"} **Status:** working draft, August 2026. Scopes the frontend tier of `paigasus-core`: app topology, session ownership, shared packages, service discovery, the console↔service transport, and the canonical error model. Opinionated; alternatives are called out where they matter. **Relationship to prior scoping:** explicitly deferred this in its *What this scopes, what it doesn't* section — *"Frontend architecture beyond 'Next.js console exists' — needs its own design."* This document is that design. It **completes** two things that document already anticipated but which were never built: the `paigasus.common.v1` canonical error envelope (§ 5 here), and the Connect-over-gRPC TS client path it described in its § 2 (§ 4 here). --- ## 0. Decisions at a glance
# Decision Choice
F1 App topology **Multi-zone**: one app per backend service, separate images and deploy pipelines, path-routed behind a single origin
F2 Session ownership **BFF**: browser holds an opaque session id only; `openid-client` v6 + a Redis-backed session store. Not Better Auth, not Auth.js
F3 Auth route placement **Embedded in every app** via a shared route-handler factory — no app is a login SPOF for another. One OIDC client, one redirect URI per zone
F4 Service topology **Addresses from config, capabilities from the service.** Three nav states: absent / unreachable / available
F5 Console↔service transport **Connect-ES over gRPC**, server-side inside the BFF. No grpc-web, no Envoy, no OpenAPI/utoipa
F6 Error model **One code vocabulary, per-surface envelopes**, using `google.rpc.ErrorInfo` — identity is `(domain, reason)`
F7 UI foundation **Tailwind v4 + Radix primitives (shadcn-style)** copy-in components in `@paigasus/ui`
F8 Deploy target **Self-hosted OCI containers.** No Vercel-only features; no build-time config anywhere
--- ## 1. Topology — multi-zone behind one origin Each backend service gets its own Next.js app, its own image, and its own deploy pipeline. Ingress path-routes a single public origin; each app sets `basePath` + `assetPrefix` so static chunks never collide. ```javascript app.paigasus.io ├─ /iam/* → iam-console (image A) ├─ /gateway/* → gateway-console (image B) └─ /auth/* → handled IN-APP by both (shared cookie, shared Redis session store) ``` **Why this over the alternatives.** Independent deploy cadence and domain separation were both stated drivers. Multi-zone buys the first outright, and buys most of the second — while the single origin makes the shared session nearly free: one cookie, no cross-domain SSO dance, no CORS on any Rust service. The two rejected options and their real costs: - **Separate origins** (`iam.paigasus.io`, `gateway.paigasus.io`) with cross-app SSO via IdP `prompt=none`. True domain separation and vanity domains, but it costs **two OIDC client registrations per self-hoster** — a config burden every customer's IdP admin pays — plus a redirect round-trip on first hit of each app and a cert/DNS entry per app. - **Single app with route groups.** Simplest by a wide margin and honestly defensible for a stateless console, but it drops the deploy-cadence driver and lets one bad page red the whole build. **The cost we accept:** cross-zone navigation is a hard navigation, and ingress config becomes part of the product's deployment contract. **Reversibility:** the split between multi-zone and single-app is cheap to reverse *in either direction*, provided the shared package boundaries in § 2 are drawn correctly from day one. Those boundaries are the expensive decision; the app count is not. --- ## 2. Auth & session The load-bearing constraint: **IAM is a pure resource server.** Per , IAM validates externally-issued access tokens and performs no auth-code flow, holds no passwords, and has no concept of a session. **The frontend tier owns the entire OIDC login flow and the session.** ### 2.1 Shape The browser never holds a token. The cookie carries an **opaque session id only** — `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Path=/`, host-only on the single origin, so all zones read the same cookie. ```javascript browser ──cookie(sid)──▶ Next server (BFF) ──Bearer──▶ IAM / gateway │ └── Redis: sid → {access, refresh, exp, prn, grants} single-flight refresh lock ``` Session state lives in **Redis**, keyed by session id: the IdP access token, refresh token, expiry, principal PRN, and the memberships/role-grants snapshot from `Introspect`. Not a self-contained encrypted cookie, for four reasons: 1. **Refresh-token rotation races.** Two zones, one user, both hit an expired token → both refresh → the IdP rotates and revokes → one zone logs the user out at random. A shared store allows a per-session single-flight lock. 2. **Logout must actually revoke.** A self-contained cookie cannot be invalidated. A security-audited product needs server-side revocation. 3. **Size.** Memberships plus role grants across an org tree will exceed the 4KB cookie budget. 4. Redis is already a stack dependency with a documented trust boundary, a circuit breaker (SMA-476) and a retry budget (SMA-473) to reuse. **The cost, stated honestly:** Redis becomes a login-path dependency. Mitigation is an in-memory store adapter behind the same port for dev and single-node self-hosting, plus the existing breaker semantics for degradation. ### 2.2 Why not Better Auth or Auth.js Better Auth was evaluated seriously. Verified against current source, it offers two modes and **both** collide with this architecture: - **With a primary database.** Adds a TS ORM plus a second migration system to a repo whose entire persistence story is Rust SeaORM migrations. Its `user`/`account` tables then duplicate what IAM already owns — IAM JIT-provisions a `User` from `(issuer, subject)` and audit-logs it through the outbox — producing two user tables, one invisible to the partitioned audit log. Its `organization` plugin, the library's biggest draw, is a direct competitor to IAM M1 tenancy and M3 Cedar roles and would have to be refused. - **Database-less.** Better Auth auto-enables `account.storeAccountCookie`, and its own source comment is explicit: *"secondaryStorage holds sessions and verification, not account records, so without a primary database the account (and its OAuth tokens) only has a durable home in a cookie."* That re-opens all three cookie failure modes above, worst of all the cross-zone refresh race. Auth.js was rejected for the identity-model reasons above, not for module-scope config — in a Node container, module scope evaluates at **server boot**, which is runtime. The genuine build-time hazards are narrower: `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` inlining, and config validation executing during `next build` prerender. **What is actually being written:** `openid-client` v6 handles the protocol — PKCE, state, nonce, discovery, JWKS, token exchange and verification are all library calls. What remains is roughly 200 lines: login route (\~30), callback (\~50), logout (\~20), `getSession()` with refresh-under-lock (\~60), middleware cookie check (\~15). The security-critical cryptography stays in a conformant library. **Where Better Auth genuinely fits — deferred, not rejected.** IAM requires an OIDC issuer, so a small self-hoster with no Keycloak or Okta currently cannot log in at all. Better Auth's `oauth-provider` plugin issues JWTs with JWKS and introspection endpoints — exactly what IAM's RS256/ES256 validator already consumes. An optional `paigasus-idp` deployable would slot in as just another configured issuer with no IAM changes. Worth revisiting when a self-hoster asks; **not** worth building now. ### 2.3 Two hard rules **No authorization in Next middleware.** Middleware performs cookie-presence checks and redirect-to-login, nothing more. Real session resolution happens in server components and route handlers via `getSession()`. CVE-2025-29927 was precisely a middleware auth bypass; the pattern is structurally fragile. **The UI never re-implements Cedar.** A `can()` helper reads role grants from the session to hide affordances, and is documented as **cosmetic only**. Every action is authorized server-side by IAM, and the UI must render the resulting 403 correctly. --- ## 3. Runtime service topology A self-hosted deployment may run IAM only, IAM + gateway, or more later. The console adapts at runtime. Three properties need distinguishing, and they need different mechanisms: - **Configured** — the operator deployed this service and supplied its address. Only the deployment knows this. Nothing is discoverable without an address, and there is no service registry — k8s DNS plus Helm values *are* the registry. - **Reachable** — it is answering right now. - **Capable** — which features that version supports. A customer on an older IAM must not see UI for endpoints that 404. **Therefore: addresses come from config; capabilities come from the service itself.** Hard-coding capabilities in the console recreates version-skew bugs; discovering addresses is impossible without a registry that does not exist. ### 3.1 Service self-description `iam.proto` already carries a stub for this — `ServiceInfo { string prn }`, commented as a placeholder. Grow it in `common/v1` into a descriptor: service name, version, and a list of capability keys (`iam.authz.cedar`, `iam.apikeys`, `iam.audit`, `gateway.chat.stream`). Keys are **strings, not an enum**, so a new capability in one service does not force a bindings regen everywhere, and an old console reading an unknown key simply ignores it. The registry lives as a doc comment in the proto. ### 3.2 Discovery is lazy and request-scoped Discovery runs inside an authenticated user's request context — never at boot. This sidesteps a real problem: at boot there is no user token, so a boot-time probe would need either an unauthenticated endpoint or a provisioned service-account credential for every self-hoster. The first authenticated request populates a Redis cache (`svcinfo:`, \~60s TTL, stale-while-revalidate, single-flight like the token refresh). The login page has no nav, so nothing is needed pre-authentication. ### 3.3 Three nav states, not two
State Condition Render
Absent Not in config Not rendered at all
Available Configured + answering Normal
Degraded Configured + unreachable **Disabled with a reason — never hidden**
Hiding a deployed-but-down service is both bad UX and a destroyed ops signal: the operator needs to see that the thing they deployed is not answering. ### 3.4 Version-skew rule The console must run against **N-1 minor** of each service. Unknown capability key → ignore. Absent capability → feature off. Never ship a console that *requires* a capability released in the same version — self-hosters upgrade components separately. --- ## 4. SDK & transport ### 4.1 As-built finding IAM's HTTP handlers use **hand-written serde DTOs** (`http::dto::{OrgDto, CreateNodeBody, …}`) with no OpenAPI spec and no utoipa/aide. The gRPC surface, by contrast, is generated from `contracts/` — the same protos already feeding `@paigasus/proto`. And the gateway **already dials IAM over gRPC**: `adapters/iam/client.rs` is a tonic `Channel` (h2c in-cluster, TLS optional, `connect_lazy`) shared by `AuthnServiceClient` and `AuthorizationServiceClient`. ### 4.2 Decision **`@paigasus/sdk/iam`**** — generated gRPC clients, server-side only.** `createClient(TenancyService, transport)` over `createGrpcTransport` from `@connectrpc/connect-node`. Types come from the contract source of truth per , with the existing codegen-drift gate already protecting them. This is where the BFF shape pays off twice over: **the client runs in Node, so real gRPC is available and no ****`tonic-web`****, grpc-web, or Envoy is needed anywhere.** Connect-ES v2 also dropped its separate codegen plugin — protobuf-es v2 emits service descriptors itself — so there is **no ****`buf.gen.yaml`**** change and no new plugin**. The cost is two catalog entries. **Why not utoipa + OpenAPI:** annotating \~40 axum handlers and maintaining those annotations forever, buying nothing the proto path does not already provide. It becomes worthwhile the day the REST API is *published* to customers as a supported surface — a product decision, not a console requirement. ### 4.3 The honest gap Three IAM surfaces are HTTP-only today with no proto service: `/v1/users`, `/v1/outbox/dead-letters/*` (list/replay/discard — real ops-console material), and `/v1/authz/system-policies/{id}/retire`. Plus the gateway chat surface, which is deliberately OpenAI-compatible HTTP+SSE and should stay that way. `@paigasus/sdk/http` is a small hand-written fetch client covering those. Per ADR-0004 the three IAM ops endpoints arguably belong in the contract anyway; as protos land, this slice shrinks toward just the gateway. ### 4.4 Mechanics - **Auth propagation is mandatory.** The M2 tower middleware wraps *both* transports, so gRPC enforces bearer tokens exactly as HTTP does. An interceptor attaches `authorization: Bearer ` from the request-scoped session. - **Transports are cached per base URL; auth is per call.** Transports hold an HTTP/2 session — recreating one per request would thrash connections, and caching mirrors tonic's shared lazy `Channel`. No token ever lives in a cached object. - **Streaming:** gateway chat proxies through a Next route handler as a `ReadableStream` passthrough. No buffering, and nothing in middleware may consume the body. --- ## 5. Error model ### 5.1 As-built finding: the vocabulary exists in one of four places
Surface Today
IAM HTTP **Good.** `TenancyError::code()` → stable kebab codes (`slug-conflict`, `parent-archived`), `ErrorClass` → status, `{error:{code,message}}`, internals never leaked
IAM gRPC **No structured detail.** `status_to_grpc` stuffs the code in-band: `Status::new(code, format!("{}: {}", e.code(), e))` — the comment is candid that "tonic has no structured-error-detail convention by default"
IAM authn gRPC **No machine code at all.** `authn_status` returns static strings only
Gateway OpenAI envelope `{message,type,param,code}` — a **binding external compatibility contract**; OpenAI SDKs branch on `error.type`
A gRPC client can currently recover a code only by splitting on `": "`. That is the concrete defect this section fixes. ### 5.2 Decisions **E1 — The code is the contract; the envelope is per-surface.** All four envelopes stay. One vocabulary underneath. Unifying the wire shapes would break the gateway's entire reason for existing. **E2 — Adopt ****`google.rpc.ErrorInfo`**** rather than inventing.** Identity is `(domain, reason)`: `domain: "iam.paigasus.io"`, `reason: "slug-conflict"`, plus a `metadata` map. This disambiguates a bare `internal` across services *without* renaming the existing tested code strings. **Kebab casing is kept** — a deliberate, documented deviation from Google's UPPER_SNAKE convention, not worth the churn. **E3 — Fix the gRPC in-band hack.** Use `tonic-types`' `ErrorDetails` to send `ErrorInfo` in the `grpc-status-details-bin` trailer, keeping the message human-readable. Connect-ES reads that trailer, so the SDK gets structured codes for free. This has an **in-repo consumer**: the gateway holds `IamError::Rpc(tonic::Status)` specifically so G5 can branch on it. Changing the message format means updating the gateway's branching in the same change. **E4 — Give the authn funnel codes.** Keep its separate funnel and its static, non-revealing messages — that posture is correct. Attach a machine code to each. Since the messages are already distinct per case, distinct codes leak nothing new. **E5 — Correlation id in every error.** The highest-value item for a self-hosted product: a user reports error `4f2a…` and the operator greps it. Internal errors return a generic message plus the trace id; detail stays in logs. **E6 — Retryability as data, not inference.** `retryable` in metadata, so the SDK never hard-codes "503 means retry." Feeds § 3's degraded state and aligns with the existing circuit-breaker and retry-budget work. **E7 — Registry plus a two-way drift gate.** The canonical list lives in `contracts/proto/paigasus/common/v1/error.proto` as doc-commented constants — **this is the ****`errors.proto`**** the monorepo scoping document planned and never built.** The gate must check **both** directions: every code Rust *emits* is in the registry, and every code the console *consumes* is too. The `:observability-drift` gate only checks that names resolve, which is exactly how a metric's prose drifted across three unlinked places; the same trap applies here to code + Rust message + UI copy. **E8 — Console side.** `mapError()` normalizes gRPC `Status` details and HTTP envelopes into one union. The UI branches on `(domain, reason)` only, **never on message text**. Unknown reason → generic fallback plus trace id, which is § 3's version-skew rule again. **Scope note:** E2–E6 are Rust + contracts work, not frontend work. They touch IAM, the gateway, and proto, and warrant their own Linear issue landing before or alongside the console. The timing argument favors now: there are no external consumers yet, so this is roughly free today and expensive once anyone depends on the current shapes. --- ## 6. Packages & dependency rules ```javascript ts/packages/ paigasus-ui/ @paigasus/ui shadcn components, tokens, Tailwind v4 preset paigasus-app-shell/ @paigasus/app-shell header, nav, org/team switcher, user menu paigasus-auth/ @paigasus/auth OIDC RP, session store, route factory, getSession paigasus-sdk/ @paigasus/sdk typed IAM + gateway clients (server-only) paigasus-proto/ @paigasus/proto generated protobuf-es [exists] paigasus-kernel/ @paigasus/kernel wasm/napi bindings [exists] paigasus-next-config/ @paigasus/next-config next.config factory, eslint/ts presets apps → app-shell → { ui, auth/client } apps → { sdk, auth/server, next-config } sdk → proto ui → React only ``` Four rules carry the weight: 1. **`@paigasus/ui`**** never imports ****`next/*`****.** It stays plain React, so it tests in jsdom without a Next runtime and remains usable from the docs app. Navigation is injected — components take a link component or read one from context rather than reaching for `next/link`. 2. **`@paigasus/sdk`**** is server-only, enforced mechanically** via `import 'server-only'`. It is the code path that attaches bearer tokens; if a client component imports it, the build fails loudly instead of shipping a token into a browser bundle. 3. **`@paigasus/auth`**** splits by subpath export — ****`/server`**** and ****`/client`****.** Server holds `openid-client`, the Redis store, the route factory. Client holds `` and `useSession()`, receiving a **sanitized** session: principal PRN, display name, role grants — never tokens, never the refresh token. Subpath exports make the boundary structural rather than a review convention. 4. **The header lives in ****`app-shell`****, not ****`ui`**, because it is the one component that must understand the zone map. **The multi-zone sharp edge.** A `` from the IAM app attempts a client-side RSC prefetch against a route its own server does not have, and fails. Cross-zone navigation must be a plain ``. `app-shell` therefore exports a `` that reads the zone map from runtime config and picks `` for same-zone, `` for cross-zone. Getting this wrong surfaces as an intermittent broken nav item — miserable to diagnose, and invisible to unit tests. **Runtime configuration.** `@paigasus/next-config/runtime` reads and zod-validates env at **first request**, not module scope (module scope risks evaluation during `next build` prerender). A server component passes only a **sanitized slice** to the client: zone base paths and capability keys. Internal service URLs are cluster-internal DNS and must never reach the browser. `` guards feature UI — cosmetic only, same discipline as `can()`; the server still handles a 404 from an older service gracefully. Packages stay **source-only** (`exports: "./src/index.ts"`, `private: true`) as they are today; apps list them in `transpilePackages`. No tsup, no dist, no build step until something is actually published. --- ## 7. Build, CI, deploy - Moon project per app and package, `-ts`-suffixed ids, `layer: application` / `library`. - **`output: 'standalone'`** in the shared `next.config` factory. Non-negotiable for self-hosting — without it the image ships all of `node_modules`. - Moon `build` outputs exclude `.next/cache`, or the cache archive bloats with every build. - **New grep gate: ban ****`NEXT_PUBLIC_`**** in apps.** Enforces the runtime-config rule mechanically instead of by review — the cheapest possible guard against baking one customer's config into a shared image. - **ESLint boundary rule** for the § 6 dependency direction, plus `import 'server-only'` at the `sdk` and `auth/server` entry points. - Catalog additions (central pinning, per existing convention): `openid-client`, `@connectrpc/connect` + `connect-node`, a Redis client, `zod`, `tailwindcss` v4, Radix primitives, `cva`/`clsx`/`tailwind-merge`, `lucide-react`. - pnpm 11's 24h `minimumReleaseAge` means a same-day npm release reds CI. - Per-project tasks skip the repo gates, so the full `moon ci … --base origin/main --include-relations` run stays mandatory before pushing. ### 7.1 Prerequisites and known landmines **Nothing in the repo is containerized.** There are no Dockerfiles anywhere — not IAM, not the gateway. "Self-hosted containers" is a stated target with no implementation behind it. The console must not invent a bespoke image story; this is a prerequisite (or parallel) workstream covering all three. **`ci/affected-graph/run.sh`**** uses strict equality, and the § 4 SDK will red it on day one.** The `contracts->proto` case asserts the affected set *equals* exactly `contracts,paigasus-proto-rs,paigasus-proto-py,paigasus-proto-ts,paigasus-gateway-rs,paigasus-iam-rs`. Once `@paigasus/sdk` depends on `@paigasus/proto`, a contracts edit also affects `paigasus-sdk-ts` and every app downstream of it — and strict equality fails on *any* extra project. This is the [CLAUDE.md](http://CLAUDE.md) kernel gotcha generalized to TypeScript. It belongs in the plan as an explicit step, not as a surprise. --- ## 8. Testing - **`@paigasus/ui`**: jsdom + testing-library, no Next runtime — the payoff of the no-`next/*` rule. `jsx-a11y` is already configured; add axe assertions on the shell. - **`@paigasus/auth`**** is the highest-risk package.** Unit-test token verification against a locally minted JWKS with `jose`, then one integration test of the full auth-code flow against a containerized Keycloak. - **Capability discovery needs all three states tested** — absent, unreachable, available. "Unreachable" is the one that will be wrong, and the one an operator most needs correct. - **E2E (Playwright), deliberately small**: the auth round-trip and cross-zone navigation. The `` hard-nav bug only manifests in a real browser — that is what earns an E2E test. - **Error mapping is a table test driven off the registry**, so an unmapped code fails a test instead of rendering an empty toast. - MSW for app-level tests so apps need no live services. **Make any container-gated test fail loud, not skip silent.** `paigasus-iam`'s Docker suites `return` early and report PASS in \~0.7s having run nothing unless `CI=1`, and nextest's `0 skipped` does not catch it. Do not reproduce that pattern here. --- ## 9. As-built starting point What exists in `ts/` today: pnpm workspace + Moon, catalog-pinned React 19 / Next 16 / TS 6. `apps/paigasus-console` is a bare App Router skeleton (`layout.tsx` + `page.tsx`); `apps/paigasus-docs` is a placeholder. `@paigasus/ui`, `@paigasus/sdk` and `@paigasus/proto` are scaffolded but empty apart from generated proto output. All packages are source-only exports, `private: true`, with no bundler wiring. The existing `paigasus-console` becomes `iam-console` (or is split), and `app-shell`, `auth`, and `next-config` are new. --- ## 10. Proposed ADRs These decisions have viable alternatives and consequences, so by the criterion they are ADRs rather than guidelines. Numbers continue from ADR-0016.
# Proposed title Why it is an ADR
0017 Console topology & session ownership (multi-zone BFF, `openid-client` • Redis) Three viable topologies and three viable session libraries were on the table, each with distinct consequences for self-hosters
0018 Connect-ES over gRPC for the console↔service transport; no OpenAPI surface The ADR index's own example of an ADR-worthy decision is verbatim "Use Connect-ES 2.0 over grpc-web for the TS proto stack"
0019 Canonical error model — `google.rpc.ErrorInfo` `(domain, reason)` across HTTP, gRPC and the OpenAI envelope Cross-cutting contract change affecting all services; alternatives were inventing an envelope, unifying all envelopes, or keeping the in-band string
0020 Service capability discovery — addresses from config, capabilities from the service Alternatives were static config only, full discovery, or a service registry; it changes the proto contract for every service
0021 *(optional)* Tailwind + Radix (shadcn-style) over a full component library for `@paigasus/ui` Comparable in stakes to ADR-0009 (ESLint + Prettier over Biome); include only if the UI foundation is considered contested
--- ## What this scopes, what it doesn't This document is opinionated on **app topology, session ownership, package boundaries, service discovery, transport, and the error model**. It deliberately does not scope: - **Information architecture and visual design** — what screens exist, navigation hierarchy, the design language itself. That is a product design exercise. - **Containerization and deployment manifests** — Dockerfiles and Helm charts for the whole stack, not just the frontend. A prerequisite workstream (§ 7.1). - **The gateway playground's product surface** — model selection, prompt history, usage analytics. - **i18n** — the error-copy registry is keyed by code and therefore i18n-ready, but no locale strategy is chosen. - **A bundled IdP** for self-hosters without one (§ 2.2) — a real future option, deliberately deferred. Scopes the frontend tier of `paigasus-core`: app topology, session ownership, shared packages, service discovery, the console↔service transport, and the canonical error model. Opinionated; alternatives are called out where they matter. **Relationship to prior scoping:** explicitly deferred this in its *What this scopes, what it doesn't* section — *"Frontend architecture beyond 'Next.js console exists' — needs its own design."* This document is that design. It **completes** two things that document already anticipated but which were never built: the `paigasus.common.v1` canonical error envelope (§ 5 here), and the Connect-over-gRPC TS client path it described in its § 2 (§ 4 here). --- ## 0. Decisions at a glance
# Decision Choice
F1 App topology **Multi-zone**: one app per backend service, separate images and deploy pipelines, path-routed behind a single origin
F2 Session ownership **BFF**: browser holds an opaque session id only; `openid-client` v6 + a Redis-backed session store. Not Better Auth, not Auth.js
F3 Auth route placement **Embedded in every app** via a shared route-handler factory — no app is a login SPOF for another. One OIDC client, one redirect URI per zone
F4 Service topology **Addresses from config, capabilities from the service.** Three nav states: absent / unreachable / available
F5 Console↔service transport **Connect-ES over gRPC**, server-side inside the BFF. No grpc-web, no Envoy, no OpenAPI/utoipa
F6 Error model **One code vocabulary, per-surface envelopes**, using `google.rpc.ErrorInfo` — identity is `(domain, reason)`
F7 UI foundation **Tailwind v4 + Radix primitives (shadcn-style)** copy-in components in `@paigasus/ui`
F8 Deploy target **Self-hosted OCI containers.** No Vercel-only features; no build-time config anywhere
--- ## 1. Topology — multi-zone behind one origin Each backend service gets its own Next.js app, its own image, and its own deploy pipeline. Ingress path-routes a single public origin; each app sets `basePath` + `assetPrefix` so static chunks never collide. ```javascript app.paigasus.io ├─ /iam/* → iam-console (image A) ├─ /gateway/* → gateway-console (image B) └─ /auth/* → handled IN-APP by both (shared cookie, shared Redis session store) ``` **Why this over the alternatives.** Independent deploy cadence and domain separation were both stated drivers. Multi-zone buys the first outright, and buys most of the second — while the single origin makes the shared session nearly free: one cookie, no cross-domain SSO dance, no CORS on any Rust service. The two rejected options and their real costs: - **Separate origins** (`iam.paigasus.io`, `gateway.paigasus.io`) with cross-app SSO via IdP `prompt=none`. True domain separation and vanity domains, but it costs **two OIDC client registrations per self-hoster** — a config burden every customer's IdP admin pays — plus a redirect round-trip on first hit of each app and a cert/DNS entry per app. - **Single app with route groups.** Simplest by a wide margin and honestly defensible for a stateless console, but it drops the deploy-cadence driver and lets one bad page red the whole build. **The cost we accept:** cross-zone navigation is a hard navigation, and ingress config becomes part of the product's deployment contract. **Reversibility:** the split between multi-zone and single-app is cheap to reverse *in either direction*, provided the shared package boundaries in § 2 are drawn correctly from day one. Those boundaries are the expensive decision; the app count is not. --- ## 2. Auth & session The load-bearing constraint: **IAM is a pure resource server.** Per , IAM validates externally-issued access tokens and performs no auth-code flow, holds no passwords, and has no concept of a session. **The frontend tier owns the entire OIDC login flow and the session.** ### 2.1 Shape The browser never holds a token. The cookie carries an **opaque session id only** — `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Path=/`, host-only on the single origin, so all zones read the same cookie. ```javascript browser ──cookie(sid)──▶ Next server (BFF) ──Bearer──▶ IAM / gateway │ └── Redis: sid → {access, refresh, exp, prn, grants} single-flight refresh lock ``` Session state lives in **Redis**, keyed by session id: the IdP access token, refresh token, expiry, principal PRN, and the memberships/role-grants snapshot from `Introspect`. Not a self-contained encrypted cookie, for four reasons: 1. **Refresh-token rotation races.** Two zones, one user, both hit an expired token → both refresh → the IdP rotates and revokes → one zone logs the user out at random. A shared store allows a per-session single-flight lock. 2. **Logout must actually revoke.** A self-contained cookie cannot be invalidated. A security-audited product needs server-side revocation. 3. **Size.** Memberships plus role grants across an org tree will exceed the 4KB cookie budget. 4. Redis is already a stack dependency with a documented trust boundary, a circuit breaker (SMA-476) and a retry budget (SMA-473) to reuse. **The cost, stated honestly:** Redis becomes a login-path dependency. Mitigation is an in-memory store adapter behind the same port for dev and single-node self-hosting, plus the existing breaker semantics for degradation. ### 2.2 Why not Better Auth or Auth.js Better Auth was evaluated seriously. Verified against current source, it offers two modes and **both** collide with this architecture: - **With a primary database.** Adds a TS ORM plus a second migration system to a repo whose entire persistence story is Rust SeaORM migrations. Its `user`/`account` tables then duplicate what IAM already owns — IAM JIT-provisions a `User` from `(issuer, subject)` and audit-logs it through the outbox — producing two user tables, one invisible to the partitioned audit log. Its `organization` plugin, the library's biggest draw, is a direct competitor to IAM M1 tenancy and M3 Cedar roles and would have to be refused. - **Database-less.** Better Auth auto-enables `account.storeAccountCookie`, and its own source comment is explicit: *"secondaryStorage holds sessions and verification, not account records, so without a primary database the account (and its OAuth tokens) only has a durable home in a cookie."* That re-opens all three cookie failure modes above, worst of all the cross-zone refresh race. Auth.js was rejected for the identity-model reasons above, not for module-scope config — in a Node container, module scope evaluates at **server boot**, which is runtime. The genuine build-time hazards are narrower: `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` inlining, and config validation executing during `next build` prerender. **What is actually being written:** `openid-client` v6 handles the protocol — PKCE, state, nonce, discovery, JWKS, token exchange and verification are all library calls. What remains is roughly 200 lines: login route (\~30), callback (\~50), logout (\~20), `getSession()` with refresh-under-lock (\~60), middleware cookie check (\~15). The security-critical cryptography stays in a conformant library. **Where Better Auth genuinely fits — deferred, not rejected.** IAM requires an OIDC issuer, so a small self-hoster with no Keycloak or Okta currently cannot log in at all. Better Auth's `oauth-provider` plugin issues JWTs with JWKS and introspection endpoints — exactly what IAM's RS256/ES256 validator already consumes. An optional `paigasus-idp` deployable would slot in as just another configured issuer with no IAM changes. Worth revisiting when a self-hoster asks; **not** worth building now. ### 2.3 Two hard rules **No authorization in Next middleware.** Middleware performs cookie-presence checks and redirect-to-login, nothing more. Real session resolution happens in server components and route handlers via `getSession()`. CVE-2025-29927 was precisely a middleware auth bypass; the pattern is structurally fragile. **The UI never re-implements Cedar.** A `can()` helper reads role grants from the session to hide affordances, and is documented as **cosmetic only**. Every action is authorized server-side by IAM, and the UI must render the resulting 403 correctly. --- ## 3. Runtime service topology A self-hosted deployment may run IAM only, IAM + gateway, or more later. The console adapts at runtime. Three properties need distinguishing, and they need different mechanisms: - **Configured** — the operator deployed this service and supplied its address. Only the deployment knows this. Nothing is discoverable without an address, and there is no service registry — k8s DNS plus Helm values *are* the registry. - **Reachable** — it is answering right now. - **Capable** — which features that version supports. A customer on an older IAM must not see UI for endpoints that 404. **Therefore: addresses come from config; capabilities come from the service itself.** Hard-coding capabilities in the console recreates version-skew bugs; discovering addresses is impossible without a registry that does not exist. ### 3.1 Service self-description `iam.proto` already carries a stub for this — `ServiceInfo { string prn }`, commented as a placeholder. Grow it in `common/v1` into a descriptor: service name, version, and a list of capability keys (`iam.authz.cedar`, `iam.apikeys`, `iam.audit`, `gateway.chat.stream`). Keys are **strings, not an enum**, so a new capability in one service does not force a bindings regen everywhere, and an old console reading an unknown key simply ignores it. The registry lives as a doc comment in the proto. ### 3.2 Discovery is lazy and request-scoped Discovery runs inside an authenticated user's request context — never at boot. This sidesteps a real problem: at boot there is no user token, so a boot-time probe would need either an unauthenticated endpoint or a provisioned service-account credential for every self-hoster. The first authenticated request populates a Redis cache (`svcinfo:`, \~60s TTL, stale-while-revalidate, single-flight like the token refresh). The login page has no nav, so nothing is needed pre-authentication. ### 3.3 Three nav states, not two
State Condition Render
Absent Not in config Not rendered at all
Available Configured + answering Normal
Degraded Configured + unreachable **Disabled with a reason — never hidden**
Hiding a deployed-but-down service is both bad UX and a destroyed ops signal: the operator needs to see that the thing they deployed is not answering. ### 3.4 Version-skew rule The console must run against **N-1 minor** of each service. Unknown capability key → ignore. Absent capability → feature off. Never ship a console that *requires* a capability released in the same version — self-hosters upgrade components separately. --- ## 4. SDK & transport ### 4.1 As-built finding IAM's HTTP handlers use **hand-written serde DTOs** (`http::dto::{OrgDto, CreateNodeBody, …}`) with no OpenAPI spec and no utoipa/aide. The gRPC surface, by contrast, is generated from `contracts/` — the same protos already feeding `@paigasus/proto`. And the gateway **already dials IAM over gRPC**: `adapters/iam/client.rs` is a tonic `Channel` (h2c in-cluster, TLS optional, `connect_lazy`) shared by `AuthnServiceClient` and `AuthorizationServiceClient`. ### 4.2 Decision **`@paigasus/sdk/iam`**** — generated gRPC clients, server-side only.** `createClient(TenancyService, transport)` over `createGrpcTransport` from `@connectrpc/connect-node`. Types come from the contract source of truth per , with the existing codegen-drift gate already protecting them. This is where the BFF shape pays off twice over: **the client runs in Node, so real gRPC is available and no ****`tonic-web`****, grpc-web, or Envoy is needed anywhere.** Connect-ES v2 also dropped its separate codegen plugin — protobuf-es v2 emits service descriptors itself — so there is **no ****`buf.gen.yaml`**** change and no new plugin**. The cost is two catalog entries. **Why not utoipa + OpenAPI:** annotating \~40 axum handlers and maintaining those annotations forever, buying nothing the proto path does not already provide. It becomes worthwhile the day the REST API is *published* to customers as a supported surface — a product decision, not a console requirement. ### 4.3 The honest gap Three IAM surfaces are HTTP-only today with no proto service: `/v1/users`, `/v1/outbox/dead-letters/*` (list/replay/discard — real ops-console material), and `/v1/authz/system-policies/{id}/retire`. Plus the gateway chat surface, which is deliberately OpenAI-compatible HTTP+SSE and should stay that way. `@paigasus/sdk/http` is a small hand-written fetch client covering those. Per ADR-0004 the three IAM ops endpoints arguably belong in the contract anyway; as protos land, this slice shrinks toward just the gateway. ### 4.4 Mechanics - **Auth propagation is mandatory.** The M2 tower middleware wraps *both* transports, so gRPC enforces bearer tokens exactly as HTTP does. An interceptor attaches `authorization: Bearer ` from the request-scoped session. - **Transports are cached per base URL; auth is per call.** Transports hold an HTTP/2 session — recreating one per request would thrash connections, and caching mirrors tonic's shared lazy `Channel`. No token ever lives in a cached object. - **Streaming:** gateway chat proxies through a Next route handler as a `ReadableStream` passthrough. No buffering, and nothing in middleware may consume the body. --- ## 5. Error model ### 5.1 As-built finding: the vocabulary exists in one of four places
Surface Today
IAM HTTP **Good.** `TenancyError::code()` → stable kebab codes (`slug-conflict`, `parent-archived`), `ErrorClass` → status, `{error:{code,message}}`, internals never leaked
IAM gRPC **No structured detail.** `status_to_grpc` stuffs the code in-band: `Status::new(code, format!("{}: {}", e.code(), e))` — the comment is candid that "tonic has no structured-error-detail convention by default"
IAM authn gRPC **No machine code at all.** `authn_status` returns static strings only
Gateway OpenAI envelope `{message,type,param,code}` — a **binding external compatibility contract**; OpenAI SDKs branch on `error.type`
A gRPC client can currently recover a code only by splitting on `": "`. That is the concrete defect this section fixes. ### 5.2 Decisions **E1 — The code is the contract; the envelope is per-surface.** All four envelopes stay. One vocabulary underneath. Unifying the wire shapes would break the gateway's entire reason for existing. **E2 — Adopt ****`google.rpc.ErrorInfo`**** rather than inventing.** Identity is `(domain, reason)`: `domain: "iam.paigasus.io"`, `reason: "slug-conflict"`, plus a `metadata` map. This disambiguates a bare `internal` across services *without* renaming the existing tested code strings. **Kebab casing is kept** — a deliberate, documented deviation from Google's UPPER_SNAKE convention, not worth the churn. **E3 — Fix the gRPC in-band hack.** Use `tonic-types`' `ErrorDetails` to send `ErrorInfo` in the `grpc-status-details-bin` trailer, keeping the message human-readable. Connect-ES reads that trailer, so the SDK gets structured codes for free. This has an **in-repo consumer**: the gateway holds `IamError::Rpc(tonic::Status)` specifically so G5 can branch on it. Changing the message format means updating the gateway's branching in the same change. **E4 — Give the authn funnel codes.** Keep its separate funnel and its static, non-revealing messages — that posture is correct. Attach a machine code to each. Since the messages are already distinct per case, distinct codes leak nothing new. **E5 — Correlation id in every error.** The highest-value item for a self-hosted product: a user reports error `4f2a…` and the operator greps it. Internal errors return a generic message plus the trace id; detail stays in logs. **E6 — Retryability as data, not inference.** `retryable` in metadata, so the SDK never hard-codes "503 means retry." Feeds § 3's degraded state and aligns with the existing circuit-breaker and retry-budget work. **E7 — Registry plus a two-way drift gate.** The canonical list lives in `contracts/proto/paigasus/common/v1/error.proto` as doc-commented constants — **this is the ****`errors.proto`**** the monorepo scoping document planned and never built.** The gate must check **both** directions: every code Rust *emits* is in the registry, and every code the console *consumes* is too. The `:observability-drift` gate only checks that names resolve, which is exactly how a metric's prose drifted across three unlinked places; the same trap applies here to code + Rust message + UI copy. **E8 — Console side.** `mapError()` normalizes gRPC `Status` details and HTTP envelopes into one union. The UI branches on `(domain, reason)` only, **never on message text**. Unknown reason → generic fallback plus trace id, which is § 3's version-skew rule again. **Scope note:** E2–E6 are Rust + contracts work, not frontend work. They touch IAM, the gateway, and proto, and warrant their own Linear issue landing before or alongside the console. No tsup, no dist, no build step until something is actually published. --- ## 7. Build, CI, deploy - Moon project per app and package, `-ts`-suffixed ids, `layer: application` / `library`. - **`output: 'standalone'`** in the shared `next.config` factory. Non-negotiable for self-hosting — without it the image ships all of `node_modules`. - Moon `build` outputs exclude `.next/cache`, or the cache archive bloats with every build. - **New grep gate: ban ****`NEXT_PUBLIC_`**** in apps.** Enforces the runtime-config rule mechanically instead of by review — the cheapest possible guard against baking one customer's config into a shared image. - **ESLint boundary rule** for the § 6 dependency direction, plus `import 'server-only'` at the `sdk` and `auth/server` entry points. - Catalog additions (central pinning, per existing convention): `openid-client`, `@connectrpc/connect` + `connect-node`, a Redis client, `zod`, `tailwindcss` v4, Radix primitives, `cva`/`clsx`/`tailwind-merge`, `lucide-react`. - pnpm 11's 24h `minimumReleaseAge` means a same-day npm release reds CI. - Per-project tasks skip the repo gates, so the full `moon ci … --base origin/main --include-relations` run stays mandatory before pushing. ### 7.1 Prerequisites and known landmines **Nothing in the repo is containerized.** There are no Dockerfiles anywhere — not IAM, not the gateway. "Self-hosted containers" is a stated target with no implementation behind it. The console must not invent a bespoke image story; this is a prerequisite (or parallel) workstream covering all three. **`ci/affected-graph/run.sh`**** uses strict equality, and the § 4 SDK will red it on day one.** The `contracts->proto` case asserts the affected set *equals* exactly `contracts,paigasus-proto-rs,paigasus-proto-py,paigasus-proto-ts,paigasus-gateway-rs,paigasus-iam-rs`. Once `@paigasus/sdk` depends on `@paigasus/proto`, a contracts edit also affects `paigasus-sdk-ts` and every app downstream of it — and strict equality fails on *any* extra project. This is the [CLAUDE.md](http://CLAUDE.md) kernel gotcha generalized to TypeScript. It belongs in the plan as an explicit step, not as a surprise. --- ## 8. Testing - **`@paigasus/ui`**: jsdom + testing-library, no Next runtime — the payoff of the no-`next/*` rule. `jsx-a11y` is already configured; add axe assertions on the shell. - **`@paigasus/auth`**** is the highest-risk package.** Unit-test token verification against a locally minted JWKS with `jose`, then one integration test of the full auth-code flow against a containerized Keycloak. - **Capability discovery needs all three states tested** — absent, unreachable, available. "Unreachable" is the one that will be wrong, and the one an operator most needs correct. - **E2E (Playwright), deliberately small**: the auth round-trip and cross-zone navigation. The `` hard-nav bug only manifests in a real browser — that is what earns an E2E test. - **Error mapping is a table test driven off the registry**, so an unmapped code fails a test instead of rendering an empty toast. - MSW for app-level tests so apps need no live services. **Make any container-gated test fail loud, not skip silent.** `paigasus-iam`'s Docker suites `return` early and report PASS in \~0.7s having run nothing unless `CI=1`, and nextest's `0 skipped` does not catch it. Do not reproduce that pattern here. --- ## 9. As-built starting point What exists in `ts/` today: pnpm workspace + Moon, catalog-pinned React 19 / Next 16 / TS 6. `apps/paigasus-console` is a bare App Router skeleton (`layout.tsx` + `page.tsx`); `apps/paigasus-docs` is a placeholder. `@paigasus/ui`, `@paigasus/sdk` and `@paigasus/proto` are scaffolded but empty apart from generated proto output. All packages are source-only exports, `private: true`, with no bundler wiring. The existing `paigasus-console` becomes `iam-console` (or is split), and `app-shell`, `auth`, and `next-config` are new. --- ## 10. Proposed ADRs These decisions have viable alternatives and consequences, so by the criterion they are ADRs rather than guidelines. Numbers continue from ADR-0016.
# Proposed title Why it is an ADR
0017 Console topology & session ownership (multi-zone BFF, `openid-client` • Redis) Three viable topologies and three viable session libraries were on the table, each with distinct consequences for self-hosters
0018 Connect-ES over gRPC for the console↔service transport; no OpenAPI surface The ADR index's own example of an ADR-worthy decision is verbatim "Use Connect-ES 2.0 over grpc-web for the TS proto stack"
0019 Canonical error model — `google.rpc.ErrorInfo` `(domain, reason)` across HTTP, gRPC and the OpenAI envelope Cross-cutting contract change affecting all services; alternatives were inventing an envelope, unifying all envelopes, or keeping the in-band string
0020 Service capability discovery — addresses from config, capabilities from the service Alternatives were static config only, full discovery, or a service registry; it changes the proto contract for every service
0021 *(optional)* Tailwind + Radix (shadcn-style) over a full component library for `@paigasus/ui` Comparable in stakes to ADR-0009 (ESLint + Prettier over Biome); include only if the UI foundation is considered contested
--- ## What this scopes, what it doesn't This document is opinionated on **app topology, session ownership, package boundaries, service discovery, transport, and the error model**. It deliberately does not scope: - **Information architecture and visual design** — what screens exist, navigation hierarchy, the design language itself. That is a product design exercise. - **Containerization and deployment manifests** — Dockerfiles and Helm charts for the whole stack, not just the frontend. A prerequisite workstream (§ 7.1). - **The gateway playground's product surface** — model selection, prompt history, usage analytics. - **i18n** — the error-copy registry is keyed by code and therefore i18n-ready, but no locale strategy is chosen. - **A bundled IdP** for self-hosters without one (§ 2.2) — a real future option, deliberately deferred. entries.name: EnterWorktree
entries.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

name.description: Optional name for a new worktree. Each "/"-separated segment may contain only letters, digits, dots, underscores, and dashes; max 64 chars total. A random name is generated if not provided. Mutually exclusive with `path`.

path.description: Path to an existing worktree to switch into instead of creating a new one. Must appear in `git worktree list` for the current repo — or, on first entry from the launch directory, for a repo nested inside it (multi-repo workspace). Mutually exclusive with `name`.

entries.name: ExitWorktree
entries.description:
Exit a worktree session created by EnterWorktree and return the session to the original working directory.

## Scope

This tool ONLY operates on worktrees created by EnterWorktree in this session. It will NOT touch:
- Worktrees you created manually with `git worktree add`
- Worktrees from a previous session (even if created by EnterWorktree then)
- The directory you're in if EnterWorktree was never called

If called outside an EnterWorktree session, the tool is a **no-op**: it reports that no worktree session is active and takes no action. Filesystem state is unchanged.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly asks to "exit the worktree", "leave the worktree", "go back", or otherwise end the worktree session
- Do NOT call this proactively — only when the user asks

## Parameters

- `action` (required): `"keep"` or `"remove"`
  - `"keep"` — leave the worktree directory and branch intact on disk. Use this if the user wants to come back to the work later, or if there are changes to preserve.
  - `"remove"` — delete the worktree directory and its branch. Use this for a clean exit when the work is done or abandoned.
- `discard_changes` (optional, default false): only meaningful with `action: "remove"`. If the worktree has uncommitted files or commits not on the original branch, the tool will REFUSE to remove it unless this is set to `true`. If the tool returns an error listing changes, confirm with the user before re-invoking with `discard_changes: true`.

## Behavior

- Restores the session's working directory to where it was before EnterWorktree
- Clears CWD-dependent caches (system prompt sections, memory files, plans directory) so the session state reflects the original directory
- If a tmux session was attached to the worktree: killed on `remove`, left running on `keep` (its name is returned so the user can reattach)
- Once exited, EnterWorktree can be called again to create a fresh worktree

action.description: "keep" leaves the worktree and branch on disk; "remove" deletes both.

discard_changes.description: Required true when action is "remove" and the worktree has uncommitted files or unmerged commits. The tool will refuse and list them otherwise.

content.text:
**Stage 0 — Intake** summary while the explorers and provisioning run:

**SMA-509 — ts: capability discovery client with three service states**

Let the console adapt to whichever services a self-hosted deployment actually runs. Addresses come from deployment config (Helm → env); capabilities come from the service's own `ServiceInfo` descriptor (landed in SMA-505). Discovery is lazy and request-scoped inside an authenticated user's context, cached in Redis (`svcinfo:<service>`, ~60s TTL, stale-while-revalidate, single-flight). Deliverables: a `hasCapability()` server helper and a `<Capability need="iam.audit">` guard component, with three UI states — absent (not rendered), available (normal), **degraded (disabled with a reason, never hidden)**.

**Status:** moved Backlog → In Progress. Both blockers are Done (SMA-505 descriptor, SMA-508 SDK). Working in worktree `.claude/worktrees/sma-509` on `feature/sma-509-ts-capability-discovery-client`.

**Constraints I found beyond the issue body** — ADR-0020 carries a **2026-08-15 amendment (A1–A5)** from SMA-505 that materially changes this work:
- **A5**: the gateway is axum-only and serves the descriptor over **HTTP only**; IAM serves both gRPC and HTTP. The amendment states explicitly that HTTP-on-both is what lets the console read both descriptors *without a gRPC transport stack*. That is in tension with the Frontend Architecture doc's §4.2 ("Connect-ES over gRPC") — for discovery specifically, the ADR wins.
- **A2**: a disabled capability's routes are *unmounted* (404 / `UNIMPLEMENTED`), indistinguishable from an older build. So "capability absent" and "capability never existed" are deliberately the same signal.
- **New consequence**: `ServiceInfo.version` reports `0.0.0` on every deployment until release-plz is activated — so the console **must not** render a skew banner driven by that field. Capability keys are the only sanctioned input to a feature decision.

**Open questions I'm carrying into the brainstorm:** which package owns this code (`@paigasus/sdk`? `@paigasus/auth`? a new one?), and how "degraded" is threaded from a server-side probe into a component that renders a *reason*.

Explorers still running. Let me note one gate hazard I found in my own lane while I wait — it will matter for the plan:

`ci/affected-graph/run.sh` uses **strict equality** on its expected task sets. There are already two anchored cases (`proto->sdk`, `proto-iam->sdk`) whose expected sets list exactly `paigasus-proto-ts:{build,test},paigasus-sdk-ts:{build,test},ts:lint`. If capability discovery lands in `@paigasus/sdk` **and** the console gains an input on the SDK, both of those sets grow by the console's tasks and the gate reds. The Frontend Architecture doc flagged exactly this class (§7.1) as "belongs in the plan as an explicit step, not as a surprise."

## package.json

```json
{
  "name": "@paigasus/sdk",
  "version": "0.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "engines": { "node": ">=24" },

  "description": "Server-only Connect-ES clients for the Paigasus IAM gRPC services.",
  "exports": {
    ".": "./src/index.ts",
    "./chat": "./src/chat.ts",
    "./iam": "./src/iam.ts",
    "./errors": "./src/errors.ts",
    "./errors/types": "./src/errors/types.ts"
  },
  "scripts": { "typecheck": "tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit" },
  "dependencies": {
    "@bufbuild/protobuf": "catalog:",
    "@connectrpc/connect": "catalog:",
    "@connectrpc/connect-node": "catalog:",
    "@paigasus/proto": "workspace:*",
    "server-only": "catalog:"
  },
  "devDependencies": { "@types/node": "catalog:", "typescript": "catalog:", "vitest": "catalog:" }
}
```

Exports are **source-only** (`.ts` files directly — bundler-resolution consumers only), all `private: true`. Five subpaths: root barrel, `./chat`, `./iam`, `./errors`, `./errors/types` (the last is the one ungitguarded, types-only entry for client components).

## Directory tree of `src/`

```
src/
├── index.ts               # root barrel, re-exports everything explicitly by name
├── chat.ts                 # ./chat entry — gateway chat client + SSE terminal-frame parser
├── iam.ts                  # ./iam entry — IAM service clients + bindAuth/createIamClient
├── errors.ts                # ./errors entry — mapError + presentation helpers (server-side)
├── server-guard.ts          # single `import 'server-only'` site
├── transport.ts             # Connect-ES gRPC transport factory + cache
└── errors/
    ├── types.ts             # ./errors/types entry — PaigasusError/Presentation types (client-safe, no guard)
    ├── map-error.ts          # ConnectError/HTTP/SSE -> PaigasusError normalizer
    ├── presentation.ts       # ErrorReason -> Presentation override table
    └── transport-status.ts   # gRPC Code / HTTP status / TransportCause -> Presentation tables
```

`tests/` (vitest, one file per concern): `chat.test.ts`, `errors-types.test.ts`, `iam-factory.test.ts`, `iam.test.ts`, `index-barrel.test.ts`, `map-error.test.ts`, `presentation.test.ts`, `server-guard.test.ts`, `terminal-frame.test.ts`, `transport-status.test.ts`, `transport-wiring.test.ts`, `transport.test.ts`.

## Connect-ES transport factory (`src/transport.ts`)

- **Exported factory**: `getTransport(options: TransportOptions): Transport` — memoized (module-level `Map` cache, keyed via `stableTransportKey`), builds via `createGrpcTransport` from `@connectrpc/connect-node`.
- **Options interface**:
  ```ts
  export type TransportOptions = { readonly baseUrl: string };
  ```
  Deliberately restricted to a single field today; `TRANSPORT_OPTION_KEYS` enumerates every allowed own key so an undeclared key throws rather than silently entering the cache key.
- **Auth**: `Auth = { readonly bearer: string } | { readonly anonymous: true }`. Not part of `TransportOptions` — it's bound per-*client* (see `iam.ts`), never per-transport, so the shared/cached transport stays token-free.
- **How a caller passes base URL**: `getTransport({ baseUrl: 'https://iam.internal:443' })` (or indirectly via `createIamClient(service, { baseUrl }, auth)`).
- **How auth reaches the wire — via an interceptor + a Connect "context value", not a constructor option**:
  ```ts
  export const authContextKey = createContextKey<Auth>({ anonymous: true }, { description: '@paigasus/sdk per-call authorization' });

  export const authInterceptor: Interceptor = (next) => async (req) => {
    const auth = req.contextValues.get(authContextKey);
    if ('bearer' in auth) {
      if (auth.bearer.trim() === '') throw new Error('@paigasus/sdk: refusing to send an empty or whitespace-only bearer token...');
      req.header.set('authorization', `Bearer ${auth.bearer}`);
    }
    return next(req);
  };
  ```
  `authInterceptor` is installed once on the cached transport (`interceptors: [authInterceptor]` inside `createGrpcTransport`); `iam.ts`'s `bindAuth` sets `authContextKey` on a per-client `ContextValues` object so each request-scoped client injects its own bearer without forking the transport.
- Also exported: `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000` (passed as `defaultTimeoutMs`), `stableTransportKey`, `disposeTransports()` (closes every cached `Http2SessionManager`, needed so `vitest run` doesn't hang).

## IAM clients (`src/iam.ts`)

- **Exported service descriptors** (re-exported from `@paigasus/proto/iam`): `AuditService, AuthnService, AuthorizationService, OutboxService, ServiceAccountService, TenancyService, UserService`.
- **Construction**:
  ```ts
  export function createIamClient<S extends DescService>(service: S, options: TransportOptions, auth: Auth): Client<S> {
    return bindAuth(createClient(service, getTransport(options)), auth);
  }
  ```
  Usage: `createIamClient(TenancyService, { baseUrl: 'https://iam.invalid' }, { bearer: token })`.
- **`bindAuth<S>(client, auth)`**: wraps a Connect-ES `Client<S>` in a `Proxy` that injects one shared `ContextValues` (carrying `authContextKey`) into every method call, and throws if the caller supplies their own `contextValues` in `CallOptions` (cross-request leak prevention). Exported for tests.
- `createIamClient` returns a **request-scoped** client — never cache it at module scope, only the underlying transport is cached.
- Also re-exports `disposeTransports` and `Auth`/`TransportOptions` types from `./transport.js`.

## Error mapping layer (`src/errors.ts` + `src/errors/*`)

- **Exported from `./errors`**: `mapError`, `ErrorInput` (type), `presentationOverride`, `grpcCodeName`, `presentationForGrpcCode`, `presentationForHttpStatus`, `presentationForTransportCause`, `ErrorDomain`, `ErrorReason` (values), and types `PaigasusError`, `Presentation`, `TransportCause`, `TransportInfo`.
- **Client-safe subset** (`./errors/types`, no `server-only` guard): re-exports `ErrorDomain`/`ErrorReason` as values plus the `PaigasusError`/`Presentation`/`TransportCause`/`TransportInfo` types — safe to import from a React client component since it never pulls in `@connectrpc/connect` as a value.
- **`mapError(input: ErrorInput): PaigasusError`** (`src/errors/map-error.ts`) is a total function over a 4-arm discriminated union — `'grpc' | 'http' | 'terminal-frame' | 'transport'`:
  ```ts
  export type ErrorInput =
    | { readonly kind: 'grpc'; readonly error: ConnectError }
    | { readonly kind: 'http'; readonly status: number; readonly headers: Headers; readonly body: unknown }
    | { readonly kind: 'terminal-frame'; readonly body: unknown; readonly status: number; readonly ids?: FrameIds }
    | { readonly kind: 'transport'; readonly cause: TransportCause; readonly message: string };
  ```
  - `'grpc'` → `mapConnect(err: ConnectError)`: reads `err.code` for a fallback `Presentation` (via `presentationForGrpcCode`), then `err.findDetails(ErrorInfoSchema)[0]` for the registry `ErrorInfo` detail (domain/reason/metadata); `presentationOverride(reason)` can override the fallback. Correlation/request ids are read from `detail.metadata` first, then `err.metadata` headers (`paigasus-correlation-id`/`paigasus-request-id`), via `firstNonEmpty` (treats `''` as "no id").
  - `'http'`/`'terminal-frame'` → `mapHttp(status, headers, body)`: parses the `{error:{code,message,param}}` envelope, maps `code` through the same `fromWireReason`/override machinery, and status through `presentationForHttpStatus`.
  - `'transport'` → maps `TransportCause` (`'timeout'|'network'|'aborted'`) straight through `presentationForTransportCause`, with no domain/reason.
  - It **never branches on `message`** — that's a pinned invariant (AC 1 in the tests).
- Never throws; `PaigasusError` is a plain serializable object (not an `Error` subclass) so it survives the RSC server→client boundary.

## Testing conventions

- **`vitest.config.ts`**: `environment: 'node'`, `include: ['tests/**/*.test.ts']`. Sets `resolve.conditions` **and** `ssr.resolve.conditions` to `['react-server', 'node', 'import', 'default']` — required because `server-only`'s exports map resolves to an unconditional-throw `index.js` unless the `react-server` condition is present (vitest 5 resolves node-environment test imports via `ssr.resolve.conditions`, not the top-level key, per an in-code note).
- **Faking the transport/server** (no live IAM service in CI): tests build a hand-written `Transport` object literal (`unary`/`stream` methods) that records the `ContextValues` each call carries, e.g. `tests/iam.test.ts`'s `recordingTransport()`, then drive it through `createClient`/`bindAuth`, or through the real `authInterceptor` directly to reconstruct the header a server would see (`headerFor`).
- **Mocking `@connectrpc/connect-node`** for transport-construction assertions (`tests/transport-wiring.test.ts`, `tests/iam-factory.test.ts`): `vi.mock('@connectrpc/connect-node', async (importOriginal) => ({ ...(await importOriginal()), createGrpcTransport }))`, with the spy itself built via `vi.hoisted(() => ({...}))` (required because `vi.mock` factories are hoisted above top-level `const`s) and given an explicit call-signature type argument (`vi.fn<(options: unknown) => Transport>`) to keep `.mock.calls[0]` typed as a 1-tuple under vitest 5.
- `afterEach(() => { disposeTransports(); createGrpcTransport.mockClear(); })` in every test that touches the transport cache, to avoid cross-test leakage and hanging HTTP/2 sessions.
- Structural/AC-style tests are common: `index-barrel.test.ts` derives the barrel's expected exports from `Object.keys` of each submodule namespace rather than a hand list; `server-guard.test.ts` parses (with the TypeScript compiler API, not regex) every export-map entry's source to assert the `server-only` guard import is first, and asserts `'./errors/types'` deliberately has none.

# B) `ServiceInfo` capability descriptor

## 1. Proto definition — `contracts/proto/paigasus/common/v1/service_info.proto`

Full contents (see file for the extensive ADR-0020 doc comments); the wire types:

```protobuf
message ServiceInfo {
  string service = 1;
  string version = 2;
  repeated string capabilities = 3;
}

enum Capability {
  CAPABILITY_UNSPECIFIED = 0;
  CAPABILITY_IAM_AUTHZ_CEDAR = 1;
  CAPABILITY_IAM_APIKEYS = 2;
  CAPABILITY_IAM_AUDIT = 3;
  CAPABILITY_GATEWAY_CHAT_STREAM = 4;
}

message GetServiceInfoRequest {}

message GetServiceInfoResponse {
  ServiceInfo service_info = 1;
}

service ServiceInfoService {
  rpc GetServiceInfo(GetServiceInfoRequest) returns (GetServiceInfoResponse);
}
```

- Service: **`paigasus.common.v1.ServiceInfoService`**, method **`GetServiceInfo`**.
- Every Paigasus service implements this. It MUST also (or instead) be served over `GET /v1/service-info` returning canonical protojson of the **bare** `ServiceInfo` message (not the response wrapper), with `capabilities` always present as `[]` when empty.
- `Capability` enum is a registry only — never a wire field type; wire strings are derived (`CAPABILITY_IAM_AUTHZ_CEDAR` → `"iam.authz.cedar"`).

## 2. Generated TypeScript (`ts/packages/paigasus-proto`)

Generated file: `ts/packages/paigasus-proto/src/generated/paigasus/common/v1/service_info_pb.ts` (protoc-gen-es v2.13.0).

- `export type ServiceInfo = Message<"paigasus.common.v1.ServiceInfo"> & { service: string; version: string; capabilities: string[] }`
- `export const ServiceInfoSchema: GenMessage<ServiceInfo>`
- `export enum Capability { UNSPECIFIED = 0, IAM_AUTHZ_CEDAR = 1, IAM_APIKEYS = 2, IAM_AUDIT = 3, GATEWAY_CHAT_STREAM = 4 }` + `CapabilitySchema`
- `export const ServiceInfoService: GenService<{ getServiceInfo: { methodKind: "unary"; input: typeof GetServiceInfoRequestSchema; output: typeof GetServiceInfoResponseSchema } }>`
- `GetServiceInfoRequest`/`GetServiceInfoRequestSchema`, `GetServiceInfoResponse`/`GetServiceInfoResponseSchema` (with `serviceInfo?: ServiceInfo | undefined`).

**Consumer import paths** — the package curates a barrel rather than exposing `generated/*` directly:
```ts
// ts/packages/paigasus-proto/package.json exports: "." -> "./src/index.ts", "./iam" -> "./src/iam.ts"
import { Capability, ServiceInfoSchema, ServiceInfoService, capabilityWireKey } from '@paigasus/proto';
import type { ServiceInfo } from '@paigasus/proto';
```
(`src/index.ts` re-exports `Capability, ServiceInfoSchema, ServiceInfoService` and the `ServiceInfo` type from the generated file, plus `capabilityWireKey` from `src/capability.ts`, a helper deriving the wire string from `CapabilitySchema.value[capability].name` rather than hand-tabulating it.)

Note: `@paigasus/sdk` does **not** currently re-export `ServiceInfo`/`ServiceInfoService` from any of its entries (`index.ts`, `iam.ts`, `chat.ts`, `errors.ts`) — a TS consumer of the SDK wanting to call `GetServiceInfo` would need to import `ServiceInfoService`/`ServiceInfoSchema` directly from `@paigasus/proto` and build a client itself via `@paigasus/sdk`'s `getTransport`/`createIamClient`-style machinery (or `createClient(ServiceInfoService, getTransport({ baseUrl }))`, unauthenticated per the gRPC handler notes below), or hit the HTTP route directly.

## 3. Rust servers (`rs/crates/services/`)

**paigasus-iam** — serves **both** transports (gRPC is the primary path per the proto's "gRPC for IAM" intent):

- gRPC: `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/grpc/service_info.rs`
  ```rust
  impl ServiceInfoService for ServiceInfoGrpc {
      async fn get_service_info(&self, _request: Request<GetServiceInfoRequest>)
          -> Result<Response<GetServiceInfoResponse>, Status> {
          let result = Ok(Response::new(GetServiceInfoResponse {
              service_info: Some(self.state.capabilities.descriptor()),
          }));
          ...
          result
      }
  }
  ```
  Mounted always (`adapters/grpc/mod.rs`), bearer-enforced automatically by `AuthLayer` (not exempted), no authorization action checked. RPC path: `paigasus.common.v1.ServiceInfoService/GetServiceInfo`.
- HTTP: `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/http/service_info.rs` — `GET /v1/service-info` (constant `paigasus_service_info::ROUTE`), inside the `protected` sub-router (inherits `require_bearer`), returns `Json<ServiceInfoDto>` built via `ServiceInfoDto::from(&state.capabilities.descriptor())`.
- Both transports share one source of truth: `Capabilities::descriptor()` in `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/service_info.rs`, which calls the shared `paigasus_service_info::descriptor(SERVICE, VERSION, &self.enabled())` helper (`SERVICE = "iam"`).

**paigasus-gateway** — HTTP only (no tonic/gRPC server at all, by design — one listening port per SMA-499 D3):

- `rs/crates/services/paigasus-gateway/src/adapters/http/service_info.rs`
  ```rust
  pub async fn get_service_info(State(state): State<AppState>) -> Json<ServiceInfoDto> {
      Json(ServiceInfoDto::from(&state.capabilities.descriptor()))
  }
  ```
  Route: `GET /v1/service-info`, protected by `require_authenticated` (not `require_iam_auth` — a valid credential but no authorization action).

**Bottom line for a TS client**: for IAM, call gRPC `ServiceInfoService.getServiceInfo({})` (or `GET /v1/service-info` as a fallback/HTTP-only client); for the gateway, only `GET /v1/service-info` exists — there is no gRPC RPC to call there.</result>

  - `'grpc'` → `mapConnect(err: ConnectError)`: reads `err.code` for a fallback `Presentation` (via `presentationForGrpcCode`), then `err.findDetails(ErrorInfoSchema)[0]` for the registry `ErrorInfo` detail (domain/reason/metadata); `presentationOverride(reason)` can override the fallback. Correlation/request ids are read from `detail.metadata` first, then `err.metadata` headers (`paigasus-correlation-id`/`paigasus-request-id`), via `firstNonEmpty` (treats `''` as "no id").
  - `'http'`/`'terminal-frame'` → `mapHttp(status, headers, body)`: parses the `{error:{code,message,param}}` envelope, maps `code` through the same `fromWireReason`/override machinery, and status through `presentationForHttpStatus`.
  - `'transport'` → maps `TransportCause` (`'timeout'|'network'|'aborted'`) straight through `presentationForTransportCause`, with no domain/reason.
  - It **never branches on `message`** — that's a pinned invariant (AC 1 in the tests).
- Never throws; `PaigasusError` is a plain serializable object (not an `Error` subclass) so it survives the RSC server→client boundary.
