## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts, writing down
what you checked as you check it:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

The scan's output is a table, not a verdict. One row for every pair of tasks
that share a file or an interface: the two tasks, what one produces against
what the other consumes, and what you found. One row for every task: whether
its own text agrees with itself — the tests it specifies against the code it
specifies, the files it creates against the files it later touches. "The scan
is clean" without those rows is not a scan you ran.

Write the table to the ledger. Rule on everything you find before execution
begins — each finding against the plan text that mandates it — and record
each ruling in the ledger. If the scan is clean, proceed without comment.
Rule on each conflict it surfaces — the spec is the binding authority, the
plan is its argument — record the ruling beside its row, and dispatch
Task 1. The review loop remains the net for conflicts that only emerge from
implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

**Batch small same-shape work.** When the plan lists several tasks that are
each a small, independent edit of the same kind — the same one-line fix,
constant change, or field addition repeated across files — do not dispatch
one subagent per task. Compose ONE dispatch brief listing every file and
its change, send the whole batch to a single subagent, and review its diff
as one unit. Reserve one-dispatch-per-task for work that needs its own
judgment, its own tests, or its own review surface.

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

**Waiting on dispatched subagents:** never poll a wait interface with
short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either.
While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review,
reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own.
When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten
minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one
line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase
any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly
all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost
child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the
  implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents —
  not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the
  report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated
  the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra
  review seat per task.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, rule on the correction, ledger it, and re-dispatch with the ruling carried in the dispatch

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is yours to rule on: weigh the finding
  against the plan text, decide with the spec as the binding authority, and
  ledger the ruling before you act on it. Do not dismiss the finding because
  the plan mandates it, and do not dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan
  without a recorded ruling.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — Ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: rule on the smallest change that unblocks the dependent work,
  ledger it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`,
  and carry it into the next task's dispatch. Parking a structural failure
  silently lets every dependent task build on it. Stop only when the defect
  leaves every path forward a guess.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or rule on the load-bearing ones and ledger what you decided. Only
the four classes above stop you here. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing `Ruling:` —
preflight rulings, parked findings, breaker adjudications, all of them — into
your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you made them, each
with what it costs if wrong. The list is exhaustive: if the ledger holds a
ruling, the list holds it. That list is the only place the decisions you
took on your human partner's behalf reach them — they read it and rework
whatever you got wrong. A ruling that dies with the workspace was a decision
made in secret.

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |
| "The implementer spawned its own reviewer — free extra assurance" | It's a duplicate seat reviewing the same diff; the task review is the gate. A worker-spawned reviewer is a defect to flag, not rigor. |

## Example Workflow

```
You: I'm using Subagent-Driven Development to execute this plan.

[Setup: worktree verified]
[Read plan file once: docs/superpowers/plans/feature-plan.md]

[Run task-brief for Task 1; dispatch implementer with brief + report paths + context]

Implementer: [Later]

  - Added tests, 5/5 passing
  - Self-review: Found I missed --force flag, added it
  - Committed

  Strengths: Good test coverage, clean. Issues: None. Task quality: Approved.

[Ledger: Task 1: complete (commits a1b2c3d..d4e5f6a, review clean)]

Task 2: Recovery modes

[Run task-brief for Task 2; dispatch implementer with brief + report paths + context]

  - 8/8 tests passing
  - Committed

[Run review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD; dispatch task reviewer with the printed path]

  - Missing: Progress reporting (spec says "report every 100 items")

[After all tasks]

[Delete this plan's workspace — the record now lives in git]

| Task | Own tests vs own code | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | vocabulary test asserts `CAPABILITY_KEYS`/`SERVICE_SLUGS`/`SERVICE_STATES` — all defined | clean |
| T2 | 11 assertions all map to exported symbols | clean |
| T3 | contract calls `writeRawForTest` — not on the interface | **F3** |

it as a real closed union in `src/types.ts`, hand-written, and extend T1's vocabulary test to
assert the union's members equal the registry-derived runtime list. — The spec's stated benefit is
the whole reason the type is not `string`; a template literal silently drops it. — Cost if wrong: a
hand-declared union can drift from the proto, which is exactly what the added test assertion
catches, so the drift is loud rather than silent.

Ruling: F2 — `SERVICE_STATES` and `CapabilityKey` are declared in `src/types.ts` directly;
`types.ts` must not import `./core/state.js` at all. — `types.ts` is the client-safe entry, and
re-exporting a VALUE from `core/state.ts` transitively pulls `@paigasus/proto` (protobuf-es) into
any client bundle importing it. That also skirts the `paigasus/boundaries/apps` ban on apps
importing `@paigasus/proto`, which the eslint rule cannot see through a re-export. — Cost if
wrong: none material; it is a move, not a behaviour change.

`DescriptorCache` interface as an optional, commented test seam, instead of augmenting the module
from `tests/cache-contract.ts`. — A `declare module` on a relative specifier is fragile and would
put a production interface's shape in a test file. — Cost if wrong: a test-only method sits on a
production interface; it is optional and documented, and the alternative was worse.

Ruling: F4 — merge T5's two import statements from `./record.js` into one. — `no-duplicate-imports`
is likely to fire under `ts:lint`. — Cost if wrong: none.

Ruling: F5 — replace T6's `make()` conditional-type parameter with a plain
`Partial<CreateDiscoveryDeps>`, and drop the `as never` cast in the unknown-key test. — The
conditional type is meaningless and `'iam.future' as never` is an illegal cast that would fail
`tsc`. With F1's closed union the argument needs a cast; use `as CapabilityKey`. — Cost if wrong:
a compile error the implementer would hit immediately.

Ruling: F6 — T8's test imports `type { ReactElement } from 'react'` and uses it unqualified. —
`React.ReactElement` with no React import does not compile. — Cost if wrong: a compile error the
implementer would hit immediately.

All six rulings are applied to the plan text before Task 1 is dispatched, so implementers read
corrected code rather than the finding plus a correction.

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will process your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

It carries two of the issue's four acceptance criteria. Tasks 1–4 already built the package, its types, the cache record, the cache port with an in-memory adapter, and the HTTP probe.

Your working directory is pinned to the MAIN checkout, but this work belongs in a worktree. Before anything else:

1. Call `EnterWorktree` with `path: "/Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-core/.claude/worktrees/sma-509"`.

All paths below are relative to that worktree root.

Read `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-10-sma-509-capability-discovery/task-5-brief.md` FIRST. It is your requirements and contains the complete, exact contents of both files. Type them **verbatim** — do not paraphrase, do not restructure, do not drop or shorten comments. This file's comments record five named concurrency invariants; they are the design, not decoration.

Follow its steps in order: test first, watch it fail, implement, watch it pass, commit.

## Interfaces from earlier tasks that already exist

`src/types.ts` — `ServiceDescriptor`, `DegradedReason`, `ServiceState`, `SERVICE_STATES`, `CapabilityKey`.

`src/core/record.ts` — `RECORD_VERSION`, `type CacheRecord`, `type Timings`, `DEFAULT_TIMINGS`, `isFresh(rec, now, timings)`, `toState(service, rec)` returning `ServiceState | null`, `parseRecord(raw)`.

`src/ports/cache.ts` — `interface DescriptorCache` with `get`, `set(service, rec, ttlMs, expectedRev)` (a compare-and-set on `rev`, `expectedRev: null` meaning insert-only, returning false when the fence loses), `delete`, `tryAcquireLock`, `releaseLock`, `close`, and an optional `writeRawForTest`.

`src/ports/logger.ts` — `interface DiscoveryLogger { event(name, fields): void }` and the `DiscoveryEventName` union.

`src/adapters/memory-cache.ts` — `createMemoryDescriptorCache(now?)`.
`src/adapters/noop-logger.ts` — `noopLogger`.
`src/probe.ts` — `type ProbeOutcome = { ok: true; descriptor } | { ok: false; reason }`.

## The five invariants this task exists to preserve

They are modelled on `ts/packages/paigasus-auth/src/core/single-flight.ts`, which you may read for reference. Each must survive verbatim into your implementation:

1. **Double-check after acquiring the lock.** Another holder may have finished between the failed read and the successful acquire.
2. **A waiter NEVER probes as a fallback.** On the lock-wait deadline it reports `degraded`/`timeout`. A fallback probe defeats the whole mechanism under exactly the load it exists for.
3. **Unique lock token plus compare-and-delete release**, so a holder whose TTL expired cannot release the next holder's lock.
4. **Release in `finally`**, and that release is itself wrapped in `try/catch` so a store error at release time cannot mask the probe's real outcome.
5. **The write is FENCED on `rev`.** A compare-and-delete protects the LOCK, never the WRITE. This matters more here than in the auth original: a background revalidation has NO wall-clock bound (`AbortSignal.timeout` bounds the network wait only — not JSON parsing, not the cache write, not an event-loop stall), so without the fence an old probe could overwrite a newer success with its own stale failure and mask a healthy service until the hard TTL.

Two further properties the tests pin:

- **A `401`/`403` outcome is NEVER written to the cache.** The descriptor is caller-independent but the auth outcome is not; caching it would let one user's expired cookie disable navigation for every user in the deployment for the negative TTL.
- **A cache read or write that throws degrades to `cache-unavailable` and never propagates.** One Redis blip must not 500 every server component rendering navigation.

| 10 | **AC3, never-settling probe, losers report timeout** | **No, for the invariant it names.** See Important 1. |

| 12 | cache throws, degrade to cache-unavailable | Partly. It reaches only the first `get`. See Minor 2. |

## Findings

### Critical
None. I found no defect that loses a write, holds a lock past its TTL, or breaks one of the five invariants.

**I1. Test 10 does not observe invariant 2. The implementer's own fix is what made it vacuous.**
The test comment names itself "THE CASE THAT ACTUALLY OBSERVES INVARIANT 2". It does not. Its timings are `probeTimeoutMs: 30` and `lockWaitMs: 60`. The winner therefore always times out and writes a `fail` record at ~30 ms, and every loser picks that record up from the in-loop re-read well before its 60 ms deadline. I counted the `discovery.lock_timeout` event, which fires only in the deadline branch:

```
6 runs, probeTimeoutMs 30 < lockWaitMs 60:  lock_timeout_branch_hits = 0   (every run)
3 runs, probeTimeoutMs 400 > lockWaitMs 60: lock_timeout_branch_hits = 7   (every run)
```

```
{"run":0,"calls":1,"losers":8,"ac3TestWouldPass":true}
{"run":1,"calls":1,"losers":8,"ac3TestWouldPass":true}
{"run":2,"calls":1,"losers":8,"ac3TestWouldPass":true}
{"run":3,"calls":1,"losers":8,"ac3TestWouldPass":true}
```

The test passes against an implementation that breaks invariant 2. Before claim 2's timeout race existed, the winner never finished, so every loser did reach its deadline. The fix was necessary, and it silently removed this test's only reason to exist. Fix: set `probeTimeoutMs` above `lockWaitMs` in this test (for example `probeTimeoutMs: 400, lockWaitMs: 60`), which I measured drives seven losers down the deadline branch on every run.

The report states that all five invariants "are still present and **independently exercised by the suite**". For invariant 2 that claim is false. Correct it.

**I2. Test 11 never reaches the branch it names.** "a loser performs one final cache read before degrading" reached the deadline branch in 0 of 5 runs. It returns `available` from the in-loop re-read instead. The test still has value, because it proves a loser picks up the winner's write, but it does not cover the final read before degrading.

**I3. Test 14 proves the adapter, not `single-flight`.** `writeRawForTest` plants `version: 99`. The memory adapter's own `parseRecord` guard rejects it and deletes the entry, so `get` returns `null` and `readRecord` never sees a record. Measured: `singleFlightSawItAsCorrupt: false`, and `discovery.record_discarded` is emitted nowhere in the whole suite. Deleting `readRecord`'s `toState(...) === null` branch would leave this test green. To reach that branch, plant a record that parses but is impossible, for example `outcome: 'ok'` with `descriptor: null`.

A slow cache now costs two extra round trips on the request path. This is forced by the AC2 test's synchronous `probeCalled` assertion, and no implementation can satisfy that assertion while keeping invariant 1 and the one-RTT path. Take this to the spec owner. The cheapest resolution is to let the test allow one tick (`await Promise.resolve()` before reading `probeCalled`), which restores the brief's detached shape. The implementer chose correctly between the code and the test, but did not report the cost.

### Minor

**M1. A lost fence with no surviving record reports the wrong reason.** In `settleProbe`, when the CAS fails and the re-read returns `null`, the function returns `degraded(service, 'cache-unavailable', null)`. The cache was available; the record expired. The reference handles this case explicitly and separately (`winner === null` means a concurrent logout there). Reaching it needs the 600 s hard TTL to lapse inside a probe of at most 1.5 s, so the frequency is very low.

**M2. Test 12 covers one throw site of four.** The broken cache rejects on the first `get`, so `resolveService` returns at once. The `tryAcquireLock` rejection, the stale-path lock rejection, and the `set` rejection are never reached by that test. I measured the `set` site by hand and it behaves correctly.

**M3. A synchronous throw from `deps.probe` on the stale path propagates and leaks the lock.** `beginProbe` calls `deps.probe` synchronously and the stale branch has no `try/catch` around it. `resolveService` would then reject, and the lock would stay held for `lockTtlMs`. The real `probeService` is documented as never throwing and returns a promise, so this is unreachable today. The cold path is protected by `probeAndStore`'s `try`/`finally`. Wrapping the stale branch the same way costs nothing.

**M4. The stale path serves the older snapshot after a fresh double-check.** When another caller revalidated between the outer read and the lock acquire, the code releases the lock and still returns `stale`, not the fresher record it just read. This matches the brief and is safe, because serving stale is allowed. It is a free improvement.

**M5. The timeout timer is not `unref`'d, and a never-settling probe is retained.** After the timeout resolves, the `.then` handlers stay attached to a promise that never settles, so the closure lives on. `probeService` always settles, so this is defensive only.

**M6. Nothing asserts `probeTimeoutMs < lockTtlMs`.** The reference documents the equivalent assertion for its holder. Here the `rev` fence makes a violation safe rather than corrupting, so a comment is enough.

**M7. The stale-path 401 rule is correct but untested.** I measured it directly and it is right. Test 4 covers the cold path only.

**Spec: ✅** — AC2 and AC3 are met, all five invariants hold in the code, a 401/403 is never written on either path, and no cache error propagates. The three deviations from the brief are all justified.

**Task quality: needs work** — for a narrow and specific reason. Two of the fourteen tests do not exercise the branch they name, a third proves the adapter instead of this module, and the report asserts that all five invariants are independently exercised when invariant 2 is not exercised at all. The `probeTimeoutMs` fix is what removed that coverage. Retime test 10, correct the report's verification claim, and raise the stale-path latency cost (I4) with the spec owner. I1 needs a two-number change; I2 and I3 need one new fixture each.

The brief's algorithm failed three of its own tests: it started no probe before returning, it hung its lock holder forever on a probe that never settled, and its write fence was a measured no-op that let a stale failure overwrite a newer success at `rev 9`. input.new_string:
Every write is a **compare-and-set on `rev`**, via a Lua script modelled on
`redis-store.ts:24-34`, and **the token is the `rev` from the snapshot taken
BEFORE the probe ran** — never a fresh read taken at write time. A losing writer
re-reads and returns the winner's state.

That distinction is the whole fence, and it is easy to get wrong. Re-reading the
record immediately before writing and using *that* read's `rev` makes the
compare-and-set agree with itself, so it never fences anything. Revision 2 of
this spec specified exactly that no-op, and it was caught by measurement during
implementation: a stale `network` failure overwrote a newer successful record at
`rev 9`, with no fence event emitted. The shape here now matches
`ts/packages/paigasus-auth/src/core/single-flight.ts`, which this section always
claimed as its model.

**A second rule, "discard a write whose probe started before the stored
`outcomeAt`", was specified in revision 2 and has been dropped.** Three reasons,
all measured: the `rev` CAS strictly subsumes it, since any newer write moves
`rev`; the CAS additionally catches a newer write carrying the *same*
`outcomeAt`, which the timestamp rule cannot; and the rule compares one
process's clock against a timestamp another process wrote, so clock skew between
two console replicas could discard a valid write.

### 8.4 The holder's own probe deadline

`AbortSignal.timeout` bounds the network wait inside `probeService`, but a
`probe` that never settles for any other reason would hang the lock holder's own
call forever — the waiters would time out correctly while the holder never
returned. The holder therefore races its probe against `PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS`
itself. A timed-out holder returns `degraded`/`timeout`, writes a `fail` record
(held for the negative TTL), and releases the lock.

docs(ts): correct the SMA-509 spec's resolution section against what was built

Implementation measured three defects in revision 2's algorithm. The reviewer
confirmed each by running the spec's own code out of tree, so the spec is
corrected rather than the code.

The important one is the write fence. Revision 2 re-read the record immediately
before writing and used that read's rev as the compare-and-set token, so the CAS
agreed with itself and fenced nothing. Measured: a stale network failure
overwrote a newer successful record at rev 9, and no fence event was emitted.
The token is now the snapshot taken BEFORE the probe ran, which is the shape
paigasus-auth's single-flight always had and which this section already named as
its model.

The second rule, discarding a write whose probe started before the stored
outcomeAt, is dropped. The rev CAS subsumes it, the CAS also catches a newer
write carrying the same outcomeAt, and comparing one process's clock against
another process's timestamp would let replica clock skew discard a valid write.

Also records that only the PROBE is un-awaited on the stale path, not the lock
acquire and the double-check. Detaching all three meant the probe never started
on a request that supplied no waitUntil. The cost is two extra cache round trips
on the stale path, stated plainly; the fresh path is still a single get.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

| available, key present | children |

input.message:
Task 9 fix round 1 of 5. Everything else verified: the reviewer mutation-tested all four structure assertions (they bite), proved commit 45b62783 is byte-identical to `prettier --write`'s output, and confirmed the README does not contradict the code. One Important finding.

FINDING (Important) — the AC4 "exposes no enforcement hook" test is a name scan, not a behavioural assertion, and it is the load-bearing assertion for AC4's strongest claim ("the server remains authoritative").

MEASURED by the reviewer: it added a genuinely blocking, throwing export to `src/server.ts` named `veto` — deliberately avoiding the five scanned words `enforce`/`require`/`guard`/`assert`/`authorize` — and `cosmetic.test.ts` stayed fully green with the blocking function sitting in the export surface undetected.

The current code genuinely has no enforcement hook (the reviewer read `src/server.ts` in full and I agree), so nothing is broken today. The problem is that the test provides no protection against one added later under any other name, while reading as though it does.

FIX — two parts.

PART 1: replace the name scan with a STRICT-EQUALITY export pin. This repo already uses strict-equality expected sets for exactly this purpose (`ci/affected-graph/run.sh` throughout, and `@paigasus/sdk`'s `tests/index-barrel.test.ts`). Assert that the sorted list of `Object.keys(server)` equals a hand-maintained expected list. Then ANY new export — named `veto`, `deny`, `block`, or anything else — reds this test until a human deliberately adds it to the list, which is the point: it forces a decision instead of sliding through.

Derive the expected list from what `src/server.ts` actually exports today; do not guess it. Write a comment above it saying it is strict equality, that a new export must be added deliberately, and why: an enforcement hook added here would silently make capability gating authoritative, which ADR-0020 says it must never be.

PART 2: add a behavioural assertion alongside it — pin the HANDLE's runtime surface. Assert that `Object.keys(createDiscovery({...}))` sorted equals exactly `['getServiceState', 'hasCapability']`. That catches a blocking method added to the returned handle, which is where gating would actually be enforced.

You may keep the name scan as a cheap extra signal, but if you do, its comment MUST disclose the limitation — that it cannot detect a hook named something outside the list, and that the strict-equality pin above is what actually provides the guarantee. A test that reads stronger than it is, is worse than no test.

PROVE IT BITES, and paste both results:
1. Add a throwing export named `veto` to `src/server.ts`, run `pnpm -C ts/packages/paigasus-discovery exec vitest run tests/cosmetic.test.ts`, confirm it now FAILS. Restore `src/server.ts` exactly.
2. Add a third method to the object `createDiscovery` returns, run the same, confirm it FAILS. Restore exactly.

pnpm -C ts/packages/paigasus-discovery run typecheck

pnpm -C ts exec prettier --check .
```
eslint must be ZERO problems and prettier must pass for the whole tree — that gate was just repaired and must stay green.

- **Docker is running**: server version 29.7.2. The container suite must actually execute; it must NOT skip.
- **Node is v24.16.0 and strips TypeScript types NATIVELY with no flag.** I verified this by running a `.ts` file directly with plain `node`. The in-memory tests already prove the single-flight ALGORITHM. This task proves the two things a fake cannot:

1. **The Redis primitives are genuinely atomic** — `SET NX PX` and the compare-and-delete release — rather than merely appearing so because one event loop serialised every caller.
2. **Single-flight holds ACROSS PROCESSES.** Two console zones are two processes, not two async callers sharing one event loop. That is why the multiprocess test forks real workers instead of running concurrent promises.

The shared contract (`tests/cache-contract.ts`, exported as `runCacheContract`) is run against BOTH adapters so a semantic divergence between the memory and Redis implementations fails in CI rather than in production. A previous review hand-traced all twelve contract cases against the Redis adapter and predicted all twelve pass — if any actually fails, that prediction was wrong and the finding is valuable, so report it precisely rather than adjusting the test.

`src/core/single-flight.ts` — `resolveService(deps, service, token)`, `type ResolveDeps`.
`src/core/record.ts` — `DEFAULT_TIMINGS`, `type Timings`.
`src/adapters/noop-logger.ts` — `noopLogger`.

- Every source file opens with `// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`.
- Prefix commands with `export PATH="$HOME/.proto/shims:$HOME/.proto/bin:$PATH"`.
- Conventional commit, workspace scope, lowercase subject ending in `(SMA-509)`. Type is `test(ts)`. End the body with:

export PATH="$HOME/.proto/shims:$HOME/.proto/bin:$PATH"
pnpm -C ts/packages/paigasus-discovery exec vitest run --config vitest.containers.config.ts
pnpm -C ts/packages/paigasus-discovery exec vitest run
pnpm -C ts/packages/paigasus-discovery run typecheck
pnpm -C ts exec eslint .
pnpm -C ts exec prettier --check .
```

Paste all five outputs.

Also state how long the container suite took and how many tests ran. A container suite that finishes suspiciously fast is the failure mode to watch for.

- Do NOT dispatch subagents. Do NOT use `run_in_background` — the container suite can take a couple of minutes; run it in the foreground and wait.
- Touch only files under `ts/packages/paigasus-discovery/`.
- **Never weaken a test to make it pass, and never add a skip-on-no-Docker path.** If a contract case fails against real Redis, that is a genuine finding about the adapter: report exactly which case and what it did, and stop rather than adjusting the assertion.

## Task 5 — Single-flight resolution with stale-while-revalidate

**Files (create):** `src/core/single-flight.ts`. **Test:** `tests/single-flight.test.ts`.

Obligations — five invariants stated explicitly in code comments:
1. Double-check after acquiring the lock.
2. A waiter **never probes** on timeout — reports `degraded/timeout`.
3. Unique lock token + compare-and-delete release.
4. Release in `finally`, itself wrapped in try/catch.
5. Write is **fenced on `rev`**; compare-and-delete protects the lock, never the write.

- `resolveService(deps: ResolveDeps, service, token): Promise<ServiceState>`; `ResolveDeps = { cache, logger, timings, now, probe, waitUntil?, sleep? }`.
- `newLockToken()`: `${Date.now().toString(36)}-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2)}`.
- `backoff(attempt)`: `Math.min(10 * 2 ** attempt, 100) * (0.5 + Math.random())`.
- Fresh record → served without probing (both `ok` and `fail` outcomes, each within its own TTL).
- Stale record (AC2) → served **immediately**, revalidation happens without awaiting; if `waitUntil` given, background promise is handed to it; a probe that **never settles** must not block the immediate return (explicit, no-wall-clock test).
- `401/403` outcomes **never written to cache**.
- Descriptor `.service` mismatch vs configured key → logs `discovery.service_mismatch` with `{configured, reported}`, no other effect.
- A write whose probe started before a newer stored `outcomeAt` is **discarded** (fenced), logging `discovery.write_fenced`; a lost CAS on `cache.set` also logs `discovery.write_fenced` and re-reads the winner.
- Any cache error at any stage → never propagate; return `degraded` with `reason: 'cache-unavailable'`, `descriptor: null`, `capabilities: []`; logs `discovery.cache_unavailable` with a `stage` field (values used: `'read'`, `'lock'`, `'probe_store'`, `'revalidate'`, `'release_lock'`).
- Corrupt record (`toState` → null) → deleted and re-probed, logs `discovery.record_discarded`.
- AC3: N concurrent cold callers on a fast probe → **exactly 1** probe call.
- AC3: never-settling probe → exactly 1 probe call; timed-out losers report `reason: 'timeout'`; a loser does one final cache read before degrading (to avoid a false outage if the winner just wrote).
- Expected PASS: **14 tests**.

## Acceptance criteria

| AC | Verdict | Test that proves it |
|---|---|---|
| **AC1 — three states, independently** | **Met** | `tests/capability.test.tsx:30` (absent renders nothing), `:36` (available renders children), `:44` (available-without-key hides), and `:87` `it.each([true,false])` for both degraded rows. The degraded tests assert presence, `aria-disabled="true"`, absence of `inert`, and a reachable `aria-describedby` text. `:119` proves activation is blocked by mouse, by keyboard, and by `defaultPrevented` on a raw `keydown`. `:111` asserts the cached descriptor survived, so row 4 and row 5 are not the same test twice. |
| **AC2 — a slow service does not block render** | **Met** | `tests/single-flight.test.ts:100`. The probe never settles. The call returns `available` with the cached descriptor, and `probeCalled` is `true`. There is no wall-clock assertion. |
| **AC3 — exactly one probe** | **Met** | Three tiers. `tests/single-flight.test.ts:130` (12 concurrent cold callers, `calls === 1`); `:153` (never-settling probe, `calls === 1`, every loser reports `timeout`, and at least 7 `discovery.lock_timeout` events prove the deadline branch ran); `tests/containers/single-flight-multiprocess.test.ts:27` (four OS processes on real Redis, summed probes `=== 1`). |
| **AC4 — gating is documented as cosmetic** | **Met, with one hole** | `tests/cosmetic.test.ts:22` and `:26` pin the export set and the handle surface by strict equality. `:45` proves a `404` degrades and does not throw. `:76` asserts the README text. The hole is finding 2 below: the README is not an input of the test task. |

The concurrency core is the strongest part of this branch. `src/core/single-flight.ts` implements all five invariants, and each one has a test that was mutation-proven to bite.

---

## Findings

### Critical

**C1 — The handle lifetime is contradictory, unenforced, and leaks one user's state to another.**

`createDiscovery` memoizes `getServiceState` in a `Map` held in the closure (`src/server.ts:78`, `:105-109`). The key is the service name alone. The token is not part of the key, and the entry is never removed.

The correct lifetime is therefore **one handle per request**. The README says this at line 71. But two other places say the opposite:

- `src/server.ts:67` says the handle "matches `createAuthRuntime()`". `ts/packages/paigasus-auth/src/runtime.ts:24-33` states in capitals: `ONE RUNTIME PER PROCESS — THE CALLER'S CONTRACT`, and supplies `getAuthRuntime` as the process-wide singleton every caller must use.
- The spec says the same at §9.1, and then says "memoized **per request**" at §9.5. The spec contradicts itself.
- The README's own usage snippet (lines 61-69) is a bare module-level `const discovery = createDiscovery({...})`. It reads as a singleton. The warning appears in the next paragraph, after the snippet.

I measured the result of a process-wide handle:

- A second caller with a **different token** received the **identical object** the first caller received. A first request with a rejected token makes every later request see `degraded` / `unauthorized`, for the process life.
- After I moved the clock past every TTL, the probe count stayed at 1. Freshness, stale-while-revalidate, the negative TTL, and the whole Redis cache become unreachable.

Nothing detects this. `createDiscovery` opens no connection and performs no I/O, so a wrong lifetime has no operational symptom. SMA-510 is the first consumer, and its author will read `server.ts:67`.

The fix is small: correct the `createAuthRuntime()` analogy, which is exactly backwards; change the README snippet to build the handle inside a request-scoped function; and record the invariant in a comment or a test. Adding the token to the memo key is a cheap second guard.

### Important

**I1 — `README.md` is not an input of `paigasus-discovery-ts:test`, so AC4's only mechanical guard can serve a stale pass.**

`tests/cosmetic.test.ts:77` reads `../README.md` and asserts it contains "cosmetic" and "not a security boundary". I confirmed the resolved input set with `moon task paigasus-discovery-ts:test`: it holds `src/**/*`, `tests/**/*`, `vitest.config.ts`, `package.json`, the proto sources and the lockfile. It does not hold `README.md`.

A commit that removes the "not a security boundary" sentence changes no declared input. Moon serves the cached pass. `repo:input-liveness` cannot catch this: it proves declared inputs are live, never that needed ones are declared. No sibling package reads its own README, so there was no precedent line to copy. The fix is one line: add `- 'README.md'` to the `test` task's `inputs`.

**I2 — The six timing environment variables have no path to the code they configure.**

`discoveryEnvShape` (`src/config.ts:79-93`) validates `PAIGASUS_DISCOVERY_NEGATIVE_MS` and five siblings. I grepped the whole repository. Nothing consumes them. There is no helper that maps them to `createDiscovery`'s `timings`, no README example that does it by hand, and no test that exercises `discoveryEnvShape` at all — `tests/config.test.ts` tests only `parseServiceMap`.

A consumer must write the six-line `SCREAMING_SNAKE` to `camelCase` mapping itself. If the consumer forgets, an operator who sets `PAIGASUS_DISCOVERY_FRESH_MS=5000` gets no effect and no error. If the consumer mis-maps two fields, `resolveTimings` catches some pairs and not others. A small exported `timingsFromEnv(config)` closes this, or the README must show the mapping.

**I3 — The README documents no use of `<Capability>` or `hasCapability`.**

`<Capability>` is the package's main product, and no application uses it yet. The README covers the states, the configuration, `createDiscovery`, `waitUntil` and the app-shell rule. It shows no `<Capability>` example, does not mention the `degraded` render prop, and does not document `data-capability-state` and `data-capability-reason`. §9.6 of the spec makes those two attributes the whole styling contract, because the package ships no Tailwind classes deliberately. SMA-510 must style the disabled state and has no written contract to style against.

**I4 — The spec still disagrees with the code in four places.**

Commit `711ca91d` corrected §8 only. These remain stale, and the spec is the binding authority:

- §9.4 shows `<Capability need="iam.audit">`. The shipped component requires `discovery` and `token` as well (`src/react.tsx:12-19`). The plan had this right; only the spec is wrong.
- §9.5 says memoization runs "via React's `cache()` when available and an injected request-scoped map otherwise". The code uses neither. It uses a closure `Map`.
- §9.3 says `CapabilityKey` is "derived from the `Capability` enum". It is hand-declared (`src/types.ts:62`) and pinned by `tests/vocabulary.test.ts:40`. Ledger ruling F1 made this choice deliberately, but the spec was never updated.
- §4's file tree puts `ServiceState`, `DegradedReason` and `SERVICE_STATES` in `core/state.ts`. They live in `types.ts`, for the reason ruling F2 gives.

### Minor

- **M1 — `discovery.record_discarded` does not fire for the case its own documentation names.** `src/ports/logger.ts:24` describes it as "a stored record was unparseable or from another schema version". Its only emission site is `single-flight.ts:95`, which fires for a different case: a record that parses but is internally impossible. Both adapters discard a foreign-version record silently (`memory-cache.ts:34-36`, `redis-cache.ts:65-70`), because they hold no logger. The rolling upgrade that `version: 1` exists for therefore produces no signal at all.
- **M2 — Seven unreachable fallbacks.** `toState(...) ?? degraded(...)` appears at `single-flight.ts:166, 173, 192, 240, 245, 321, 328`. `readRecord` already deletes every record for which `toState` returns `null`, and `recordFor` never builds one. The `??` arms exist only to narrow `ServiceState | null`. They are defensive, not wrong, but no test can reach them.
- **M3 — `deps.services[service] ?? ''` (`server.ts:84`) is unreachable.** `getServiceState` returns `absent` before the probe is built.
- **M4 — `resolveService` can reject if an injected logger throws.** `logger.event` is called unguarded at `single-flight.ts:235` and `:319`, outside any enclosing `try`. This is the one route by which deferred minor 3 becomes reachable.
- **M5 — `serviceOf` sits in the one module that imports `@paigasus/proto` as a value.** `react.tsx` imports `core/state.ts` only to reach a three-line pure string function, and so pulls protobuf-es with it. This is safe, because `react.tsx` is `server-only`. It is still the coupling that `types.ts` documents at length as the thing to avoid.
- **M6 — An empty token still takes the cold-path lock.** Spec §7.2 says the cache is "served read-only" for an absent token. `probeService` short-circuits without a network call, so the lock is held for microseconds only, but the lock write does happen.
- **M7 (pre-existing, not this branch) — `typecheck` compiles `tests/**` but keys only on `src/**/*`.** `paigasus-sdk`, `paigasus-auth` and `paigasus-ui` all have the same shape. Do not fix it here.

---

`createDiscovery` memoizes `getServiceState` in a `Map` held in the closure (`src/server.ts:78`, `:105-109`). The key is the service name alone. The token is not part of the key, and the entry is never removed.

The correct lifetime is therefore **one handle per request**. The README says this at line 71. But two other places say the opposite:

- `src/server.ts:67` says the handle "matches `createAuthRuntime()`". `ts/packages/paigasus-auth/src/runtime.ts:24-33` states in capitals: `ONE RUNTIME PER PROCESS — THE CALLER'S CONTRACT`, and supplies `getAuthRuntime` as the process-wide singleton every caller must use.

- The README's own usage snippet (lines 61-69) is a bare module-level `const discovery = createDiscovery({...})`. It reads as a singleton. The warning appears in the next paragraph, after the snippet.

- A second caller with a **different token** received the **identical object** the first caller received. A first request with a rejected token makes every later request see `degraded` / `unauthorized`, for the process life.

1	# SMA-509 — `@paigasus/discovery`: capability discovery with three service states
2	
3	**Status:** approved design, revision 2 (after adversarial challenge)
4	**Date:** 2026-09-10
5	**Issue:** [SMA-509](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-509/ts-capability-discovery-client-with-three-service-states)
6	**ADR:** ADR-0020 — Service capability discovery, including its 2026-08-15 amendment (A1–A5)
7	**Depends on:** SMA-505 (descriptor, Done), SMA-508 (`@paigasus/sdk`, Done)
8	**Blocks:** SMA-510 (`@paigasus/app-shell`)
9	
10	---
11	
12	## 1. Problem
13	
14	`paigasus-core` is self-hostable. A deployment may run IAM alone, IAM and the
15	gateway, or more services later. The console must adapt at runtime.
16	
17	Three properties need different mechanisms:
18	
19	- **Configured** — the operator deployed the service and supplied its address.
20	  Only the deployment knows this.
21	- **Reachable** — the service answers now.
22	- **Capable** — which features that build supports.
23	
24	Addresses come from deployment configuration. Capabilities come from the service
25	itself, through the `ServiceInfo` descriptor that SMA-505 landed.
26	
27	---
28	
29	## 2. Scope
30	
31	This issue delivers **package code only**. It does not wire authentication or
32	discovery into `paigasus-console`.
33	
34	The console today depends on `@paigasus/next-config` and `@paigasus/ui` only. It
35	has no `middleware.ts`, no auth route handler, and no `getSession()` call, so
36	`@paigasus/auth` (SMA-506) is not wired into the app. Discovery must run inside
37	an authenticated request context, so it cannot run in the console as it stands.
38	
39	**In scope:** the package, its public API, its cache, its tests, and the repo
40	gate changes the new package forces.
41	
42	**Out of scope:** console wiring, the OIDC flow, a navigation component, and the
43	choice of whether production shares one Redis connection with `@paigasus/auth`.
44	
45	### 2.1 How SMA-510 consumes this
46	
47	`<Capability>` is an **async server component**. The ESLint block
48	`paigasus/boundaries/app-shell` (`ts/packages/paigasus-next-config/src/eslint.mjs:107-116`)
49	bans `@paigasus/sdk` and `@paigasus/auth/server` from `@paigasus/app-shell`
50	because app-shell is client-reachable.
51	
52	Therefore **app-shell must not import `@paigasus/discovery/react`.** The division
53	is:
54	
55	- `@paigasus/app-shell` exports navigation **presentation** that takes resolved
56	  state as props. It stays client-reachable.
57	- The **app** composes `<Capability>` around app-shell's presentation
58	  components, because only the app has a server request context.
59	
60	This constraint is recorded here so SMA-510 does not discover it late.
61	
62	---
63	
64	## 3. Facts established before design
65	
66	These come from the code and the ADRs. They are not open questions.
67	
68	**F1 — The transport is HTTP for both services.**
69	`contracts/proto/paigasus/common/v1/service_info.proto` defines
70	`ServiceInfoService.GetServiceInfo`. IAM serves it over gRPC and over
71	`GET /v1/service-info`. The gateway has no gRPC server at all; it is axum-only
72	and serves `GET /v1/service-info` alone. ADR-0020 A5 states that serving HTTP on
73	both is what lets the console read both descriptors without a gRPC transport
74	stack. One call shape covers both services.
75	
76	**F2 — Both routes are authenticated but not authorized.**
77	IAM's route sits in the `protected` sub-router behind `require_bearer`. The
78	gateway's uses `require_authenticated`, not `require_iam_auth`. Per ADR-0020 A4,
79	a validated token whose identity is not yet provisioned counts as authenticated
80	on the discovery path. The descriptor is byte-identical for every caller.
81	
82	**F3 — `version` carries no signal for these two services.**
83	`paigasus-gateway` and `paigasus-iam` are pinned at `version = "0.0.0"`
84	**deliberately**: `env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")` feeds `ServiceInfo`, and ADR-0020
85	skew reporting is parked on that value (SMA-505 R7). release-plz has since cut
86	its first live release (SMA-580), but it tagged only the kernel family, not
87	these crates. The console must not render a version-skew banner. Capability keys
88	are the only sanctioned input to a feature decision.
89	
90	**F4 — A disabled capability is indistinguishable from an old build.**
91	Per ADR-0020 A2, a disabled capability's HTTP routes are not registered (`404`)
92	and its gRPC RPCs return `UNIMPLEMENTED`. The client cannot tell "turned off"
93	from "not built yet", and does not need to.
94	
95	**F5 — `@paigasus/auth` owns the only Redis connection.**
96	`createRedisSessionStore()` runs once inside a memoized `createAuthRuntime()`.
97	Its `SessionStore` port is session-shaped and `core/single-flight.ts` is written
98	against `SessionRecord`. Neither is a general cache, so neither is reused
99	directly.
100	
101	**F6 — There is no UI pattern to inherit.**
102	`@paigasus/ui` has no Button, no Tooltip, and no "disabled with a reason"
103	component.
104	
105	**F7 — The cache key's `<service>` is fixed by a proto MUST.**
106	`service_info.proto:84-94` states that `ServiceInfo.service` is **advisory and
107	never a cache key**, and that the `<service>` in `svcinfo:<service>` "MUST be the
108	client's own deployment configuration identifier for the service it dialled,
109	never this server-reported value — otherwise a misconfigured or hostile service
110	could poison another service's cache entry. A mismatch is worth logging and
111	nothing more."
112	
113	**F8 — `@paigasus/sdk`'s `Presentation` union cannot express a degraded reason.**
114	`ts/packages/paigasus-sdk/src/errors/types.ts:22` fixes it at
115	`'relogin' | 'forbidden' | 'not-found' | 'degraded' | 'rate-limited' |
116	'invalid-input' | 'conflict' | 'disabled' | 'generic'`. `HTTP_TABLE`
117	(`transport-status.ts:55-69`) has **no 500 row** and **deliberately no 2xx row**.
118	This package therefore owns its own reason vocabulary (§10) and takes **no**
119	`@paigasus/sdk` dependency. Revision 1 of this spec claimed otherwise and was
120	wrong.
121	
122	---
123	
124	## 4. Package shape
125	
126	A new source-only package, `private: true`, no build step.
127	
128	```
129	ts/packages/paigasus-discovery/
130	  README.md                      required by AC4
131	  moon.yml
132	  vitest.config.ts               node; jsdom per-file via docblock
133	  vitest.containers.config.ts    real-Redis project
134	  tests/support/server-only-stub.ts
135	  src/
136	    server.ts                    './server' entry, 'server-only'
137	    react.tsx                    './react' entry, 'server-only'
138	    disabled.tsx                 'use client' — the disabled wrapper
139	    types.ts                     './types' entry, client-safe
140	    config.ts                    discoveryEnvShape (zod)
141	    probe.ts                     GET /v1/service-info
142	    core/
143	      state.ts                   CAPABILITY_KEYS, SERVICE_SLUGS, serviceOf (imports @paigasus/proto)
144	      record.ts                  CacheRecord, isFresh, toState
145	      reasons.ts                 status/cause -> DegradedReason
146	      single-flight.ts           SWR + lock algorithm
147	    ports/
148	      cache.ts                   DescriptorCache
149	      logger.ts                  DiscoveryLogger
150	    adapters/
151	      redis-cache.ts             takes an injected node-redis client
152	      memory-cache.ts
153	      noop-logger.ts
154	```
155	
156	**`ServiceState`, `DegradedReason` and `SERVICE_STATES` live in `types.ts`, not
157	`core/state.ts`.** An earlier revision of this section put them in
158	`core/state.ts`; the shipped code corrects that. `core/state.ts` imports
159	`@paigasus/proto` as a VALUE (to derive `CAPABILITY_KEYS` and `SERVICE_SLUGS`),
160	and `types.ts` is the client-safe entry — re-exporting these three from
161	`core/state.ts` would pull protobuf-es into any client bundle that imports
162	`@paigasus/discovery/types`.
163	
164	### 4.1 Entry points
165	
166	| Entry | Contents | Guard |
167	|---|---|---|
168	| `./server` | `createDiscovery`, `DescriptorCache`, `DiscoveryLogger`, both adapters, `discoveryEnvShape` | `import 'server-only'` |

26	
27	---
28	
29	## 2. Scope
30	
31	This issue delivers **package code only**. It does not wire authentication or
32	discovery into `paigasus-console`.
33	
34	The console today depends on `@paigasus/next-config` and `@paigasus/ui` only. It
35	has no `middleware.ts`, no auth route handler, and no `getSession()` call, so
36	`@paigasus/auth` (SMA-506) is not wired into the app. Discovery must run inside
37	an authenticated request context, so it cannot run in the console as it stands.
38	
39	**In scope:** the package, its public API, its cache, its tests, and the repo
40	gate changes the new package forces.
41	
42	**Out of scope:** console wiring, the OIDC flow, a navigation component, and the
43	choice of whether production shares one Redis connection with `@paigasus/auth`.
44	
45	### 2.1 How SMA-510 consumes this
46	
47	`<Capability>` is an **async server component**. The ESLint block
48	`paigasus/boundaries/app-shell` (`ts/packages/paigasus-next-config/src/eslint.mjs:107-116`)
49	bans `@paigasus/sdk` and `@paigasus/auth/server` from `@paigasus/app-shell`
50	because app-shell is client-reachable.
51	
52	Therefore **app-shell must not import `@paigasus/discovery/react`.** The division
53	is:
54	
55	- `@paigasus/app-shell` exports navigation **presentation** that takes resolved
56	  state as props. It stays client-reachable.
57	- The **app** composes `<Capability>` around app-shell's presentation
58	  components, because only the app has a server request context.
59	
60	This constraint is recorded here so SMA-510 does not discover it late.
61	
62	---
63	
64	## 3. Facts established before design
65	
66	These come from the code and the ADRs. They are not open questions.
67	
68	**F1 — The transport is HTTP for both services.**
69	`contracts/proto/paigasus/common/v1/service_info.proto` defines
70	`ServiceInfoService.GetServiceInfo`. IAM serves it over gRPC and over
71	`GET /v1/service-info`. The gateway has no gRPC server at all; it is axum-only
72	and serves `GET /v1/service-info` alone. ADR-0020 A5 states that serving HTTP on
73	both is what lets the console read both descriptors without a gRPC transport
74	stack. One call shape covers both services.
75	
76	**F2 — Both routes are authenticated but not authorized.**
77	IAM's route sits in the `protected` sub-router behind `require_bearer`. The
78	gateway's uses `require_authenticated`, not `require_iam_auth`. Per ADR-0020 A4,
79	a validated token whose identity is not yet provisioned counts as authenticated
80	on the discovery path. The descriptor is byte-identical for every caller.
81	
82	**F3 — `version` carries no signal for these two services.**
83	`paigasus-gateway` and `paigasus-iam` are pinned at `version = "0.0.0"`
84	**deliberately**: `env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")` feeds `ServiceInfo`, and ADR-0020
85	skew reporting is parked on that value (SMA-505 R7). release-plz has since cut
86	its first live release (SMA-580), but it tagged only the kernel family, not
87	these crates. The console must not render a version-skew banner. Capability keys
88	are the only sanctioned input to a feature decision.
89	
90	**F4 — A disabled capability is indistinguishable from an old build.**
91	Per ADR-0020 A2, a disabled capability's HTTP routes are not registered (`404`)
92	and its gRPC RPCs return `UNIMPLEMENTED`. The client cannot tell "turned off"
93	from "not built yet", and does not need to.
94	
95	**F5 — `@paigasus/auth` owns the only Redis connection.**
96	`createRedisSessionStore()` runs once inside a memoized `createAuthRuntime()`.
97	Its `SessionStore` port is session-shaped and `core/single-flight.ts` is written
98	against `SessionRecord`. Neither is a general cache, so neither is reused
99	directly.
100	
101	**F6 — There is no UI pattern to inherit.**
102	`@paigasus/ui` has no Button, no Tooltip, and no "disabled with a reason"
103	component.
104	
105	**F7 — The cache key's `<service>` is fixed by a proto MUST.**
106	`service_info.proto:84-94` states that `ServiceInfo.service` is **advisory and
107	never a cache key**, and that the `<service>` in `svcinfo:<service>` "MUST be the
108	client's own deployment configuration identifier for the service it dialled,
109	never this server-reported value — otherwise a misconfigured or hostile service
110	could poison another service's cache entry. A mismatch is worth logging and
111	nothing more."
112	
113	**F8 — `@paigasus/sdk`'s `Presentation` union cannot express a degraded reason.**
114	`ts/packages/paigasus-sdk/src/errors/types.ts:22` fixes it at
115	`'relogin' | 'forbidden' | 'not-found' | 'degraded' | 'rate-limited' |
116	'invalid-input' | 'conflict' | 'disabled' | 'generic'`. `HTTP_TABLE`
117	(`transport-status.ts:55-69`) has **no 500 row** and **deliberately no 2xx row**.
118	This package therefore owns its own reason vocabulary (§10) and takes **no**
119	`@paigasus/sdk` dependency. Revision 1 of this spec claimed otherwise and was
120	wrong.
121	
122	---
123	
124	## 4. Package shape
125	
126	A new source-only package, `private: true`, no build step.
127	
128	```
129	ts/packages/paigasus-discovery/
130	  README.md                      required by AC4
131	  moon.yml
132	  vitest.config.ts               node; jsdom per-file via docblock
133	  vitest.containers.config.ts    real-Redis project
134	  tests/support/server-only-stub.ts
135	  src/
136	    server.ts                    './server' entry, 'server-only'
137	    react.tsx                    './react' entry, 'server-only'
138	    disabled.tsx                 'use client' — the disabled wrapper
139	    types.ts                     './types' entry, client-safe
140	    config.ts                    discoveryEnvShape (zod)
141	    probe.ts                     GET /v1/service-info
142	    core/
143	      state.ts                   CAPABILITY_KEYS, SERVICE_SLUGS, serviceOf (imports @paigasus/proto)
144	      record.ts                  CacheRecord, isFresh, toState
145	      reasons.ts                 status/cause -> DegradedReason
146	      single-flight.ts           SWR + lock algorithm
147	    ports/
148	      cache.ts                   DescriptorCache
149	      logger.ts                  DiscoveryLogger
150	    adapters/
151	      redis-cache.ts             takes an injected node-redis client
152	      memory-cache.ts
153	      noop-logger.ts
154	```
155

157	`core/state.ts`.** An earlier revision of this section put them in
158	`core/state.ts`; the shipped code corrects that. `core/state.ts` imports
